Then we will resume at is 11.20 for Counsel Puliselic, who has only one hour, until 12.20. Then a break of 10 minutes and then we will resume again at 12.30 until 2.00. It's a very tight schedule. I'm so sorry, but we can't do otherwise. Now, I think it's the turn of -- yes, Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have a question. Yesterday we made an oral proposal for temporary release while the Defence counsel of the third accused submitted this request in writing. Does that mean that we have to make our submissions in writing too or is our oral proposal sufficient?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Your oral proposal is sufficient, and I was about to say that we have carefully considered the three motions, two oral motions, one written motion for provisional release concerning Zoran, Mirjan, and Vlatko Kupreskic. We rule that they must be denied, because no exceptional circumstances is provided for in Rule 65 are present. I would also like to add that the proposal or the idea floated by President McDonald in New York to the General Assembly and the Security Council, based on a proposal by a group of experts that has recently visited the U.N. premises here at our Tribunal, that proposal relates to a possibility for provisional release at the initial stage, namely at initial appearance. If that proposal is accepted by the Plenary, then the accused, who has surrendered voluntarily to the Tribunal, may, at the initial appearance, request provisional release. It does not -- therefore, as I say, assuming that proposal is accepted by the plenary meeting of Judges, that idea does not apply to persons who are here in detention during trial. Now, in our case we -- now, today we close our proceedings so, therefore, it's a very late stage. We can now prove to our next Defence counsel. I think Counsel Susak. It is your turn, if I'm not wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It is my turn. Your Honours, my learned colleagues in the Prosecution, Drago Josipovic, who is on trial here volunteered to come before this Tribunal, in the belief that truth and justice would prevail here. Drago Josipovic is being tried on the basis of an indictment from the 9th of February, 1998, according to which he, with the other accused, in the period from October 1992 to May 1993, committed crimes in the area of Ahmici. In the amended indictment, it is alleged that there was an armed conflict in the period from October 1992 until May 1993 between the HVO and the army of B and H, and according to the indictment, the HVO, on the 16th of April, 1993, attacked Vitez and the surrounding villages and that this was a highly coordinated operation by several hundred HVO soldiers. In this context, Drago Josipovic is charged with having committed the counts of persecution, as described in paragraphs 9, 10, 20, and 21 of the amended indictment, and this is characterised as a crime against humanity. Apart from this, Drago Josipovic is being charged that on the 16th of April, 1993, together with another accused, he attacked the home of Muzafer Puscul, and that he and Vlado Santic murdered Muzafer Puscul and took away his family forcibly. It is alleged in the indictment that Drago Josipovic and Vladimir Santic did this together with a group of soldiers. In the indictment this is characterised as a crime against humanity and a breach of the Laws and Customs of War. In my opinion, there is no evidence to prove that Drago Josipovic committed any of the crimes alleged against him in the amended indictment. This follows from the evidence presented before this Court. I will refer very briefly to the general part of the indictment; the specific part of the indictment; the evidence presented by the Prosecution, the Defence, and Court witnesses. Of course, I will try to be brief, and I will try not to repeat myself or to repeat what has already been said by my colleagues in their closing arguments. The Court has heard evidence which provides a factual basis for a final judgement which will be just and to evaluate the counts which -- or, rather, the root of these allegations and their significance. It should be mentioned that relations between Croats and Muslims deteriorated due to differing attitudes to the war in Croatia. This follows from the testimony of Zvonimir Cilic and Vlado Alilovic. It is for this reason, in relation to the Serbs, that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was established in November 1992, and in the following year the HVO and the military component were established. The first conflict between Muslims and Croats broke out on the 20th of October, 1992, and this was initiated by the Muslims as can be seen from the testimony of Fahrudin Ahmic, Abdulah Ahmic, Mehmed Ahmic, Zvonimir Cilic, and Vlado Alilovic. It follows from the testimony of these witnesses that there was a roadblock set up on the Vitez-Novi Travnik road, and it was set up by members of the Muslim armed forces from Ahmici, supported by units of Vrhovine, following the orders of the higher command. The Vitez-Novi Travnik communication was of strategic importance for the HVO, as follows from the testimony of Bryan Watters; Sefer Halilovic, who was a general of the army of BH; and Asim Dzambasovic, who was also an expert witness in this trial. This first conflict is important for Drago Josipovic, because certain conclusions can be drawn from it -- whether he was a member of the HVO or not -- because the Prosecutor, in his closing argument, categorically claimed that Drago Josipovic was an active member of the HVO as a reservist. However, these categories were not quite clear to me, and in this connection I will mention that during the first conflict, Drago Josipovic's barn was torched. Witness CA, who is a Muslim, said that she helped put out the fire in Drago Josipovic's barn together with Avdo Becirevic, Fahrudin Ahmic, and Hazim Ahmic, who are all Muslims. This is important, because clear and specific conclusions can be drawn from it, that Drago Josipovic did not participate in the first conflict, that he was not an active member of the HVO, and that he had not been mobilised into the HVO at that time. This also shows that even in wartime, the neighbourly relations between Drago Josipovic and Fahran Ahmici, Witness CA, and witness CB were good. After the first conflict, there were negotiations, and this again concerns Drago Josipovic. In these negotiations, there was discussion of the return of Muslims to Ahmici and also the return of weapons. It is well known in history that a side that loses in a war lays down its weapons. The fact that this agreement was reached follows from the testimonies of Abdulah Ahmic, Witness B, Witness II, Witness FF, and Witness Q. The expert witness, Asim Dzambasovic, helped us in this respect because he said that the two sides in a conflict can agree that one side should lay down its arms. In this context, I should mention the confiscation of the rifle of Fahran Ahmic. Witness AH said that he took a rifle after the barracks belonging to the former JNA were taken, and together with Drago Josipovic, he used several barrels to make a rifle. Drago Josipovic and Fahran Ahmic together made a rifle. The witness also says that Nenad Santic took away Fahran Ahmic's rifle. However, she did not say to whom Nenad Santic gave this rifle, and this corresponds to the testimony of Witness CB, who also said that Nenad Santic took away Fahran Ahmic's rifle. However, it follows from Anto Bralo's testimony that he gave the rifle to Nikica Grebenar, who was in charge of putting people on guard duty in Zume. As to the request of Fahran Ahmic, the rifle was handed over to Drago Josipovic. This was said not only by Anto Bralo but also confirmed by witnesses Frano Kovac and Witness DH. Witness CB said that the fact that the rifle was found in Drago Josipovic's possession did not cause any tension between the two families; on the contrary, she added that Drago Josipovic visited Fahran Ahmic frequently, and vice versa. So they resolved the problem between themselves. Witness CB, who was present at these meetings, says that Drago Josipovic would have returned the rifle. I believe that at the time this rifle was taken away, Drago Josipovic did not know what would happen the following year, in April. He did not use the rifle to intimidate anyone. Let me add that Witness CB said that the rifle was taken away with a receipt, that it was handed over to the village guard; therefore, the rifle was taken away in an official manner, on the basis of an agreement to be used by the village guard. I believe that Drago Josipovic cannot be charged with this because the fact that he had a rifle, that he had a uniform, does not mean that he committed any crimes. The Prosecutor's claim that there were no members of the army of BH in Ahmici is not correct. It runs contrary to the testimony of Witnesses C, M, V, and Z. It also runs counter to the testimony of Asim Dzambasovic and Abdulah Ahmic. Abdulah Ahmic testified that Muslims of military age belonged to the Muslim Vitez Brigade, and that was the 325th Mountain Brigade, which had an organised command. Witness V said that there was an organised unit of the army of BH in Ahmici, and he referred to details contained in his diary, while Witness Y said that the staff of the 325th Mountain Brigade came back to Ahmici to help organise men and he says that several villages, on the 16th of April, 1993, took up positions in Ahmici near the mosque. It is the Prosecutor's contention that Drago Josipovic was a soldier and a member of the HVO, and that is because he was a member of the village guards. It is evident from the statement of Zvonimir Cilic that, prior to the establishment of the HVO, there had been village guards in the village. Initially, they were joint, comprising of Muslims and Croats, and after the first clash of the 15th of October, 1992, they separated. The witness Zvonimir Cilic stressed that in Rovna, in July 1992, the Muslims established their own government and the war command later in the same year, so that two governments, two police forces, and to armies functioned at the same time. The village guard in Santici was established spontaneously by the people, and there was just one person who was in charge, and that was according to an agreement between the men in question for distributing the guards, posting them on duty, and maintaining records. The village guards were organised in such a way that there were no horizontal or vertical links with the command, and this is obvious from the testimony of Mehmed Ahmic, Vlado Alilovic, Zvonimir Cilic, Fahrudin Ahmic, and Abdulah Ahmic. Witness DA stressed that the village guards did not have an official structure, nor did they have a commander, and Rudo Kurevija confirmed that there were volunteers from among the ranks of the village guards who volunteered to enlist with the HVO. It is obvious from the commands, on the order of Colonel Blaskic, that the village guards were actually outside the military setup; namely, these orders were not actually -- were not sent to the village guards, so that we cannot accept the Prosecutor's claim that the village guards were in the service of the HVO there. On the fact that I have completed by exposition on this particular issue, I would like to proceed with another item, which is the locking up and threatening of Aladin Karahodza. Witness BB and the Witness Z charged Drago Josipovic with having, on the night between the 15th and 16th of April, locked up the sentry Aladin Karahodza in the guard post, the sentry post in the warehouse of Santici, in the timber warehouse of Santici. Both witnesses stated that this was related to them by Aladin Karahodza. I have to emphasise right away that in his closing argument, the Prosecutor only used some fragments from the testimony of these witnesses, and I believe that, in principle, the seeking of material truth can be satisfied only when all the extenuating circumstances favouring the accused, as well as all the aggravating circumstances, which further burden the accused, are properly established. First and foremost, it follows from the statement of Witness Z that Drago Josipovic was not near the warehouse. He stresses that, together with Galib Imsirovic, on that very night, he was on guard duty, and he also stresses that there were reinforced guards that were also patrolling the village. His house is right next to the road, and it is some 20 metres away from the house of Drago Josipovic. But on the other side of his house, that is, the house of Witness Z, there is an asphalt road and the Ogrjev warehouse is right there. The warehouse has a white fence, which is 8 by 6 metres in diameter, so that he had very good visibility, and if they had reinforced guards until 2.00 a.m., then they would have probably seen Drago Josipovic as they passed the road, went to the storehouse, and proceeded towards the guard post. Let me add right away that Witness Z also stated that he continued to keep watch -- that the guards -- that there was a guard there, Galib Imsirovic, who continued to keep guard. The Prosecutor absolutely circumvented the part of the statement of this particular witness who said that Drago Josipovic had not been at the warehouse of Ogrjev on that specific night. This is not all. It follows from the statement of Witness Dragan Calic that Aladin Karahodza was a guard in this warehouse. It was his duty, was his assignment, to be there on guard duty until the foreman came on the next morning, on April 16, 1993, for his work, and I believe that the real reason why Aladin Karahodza did not leave the guard post was that he was just as afraid as Witness Z was, because Witness Z said that after the shooting, he was in his house and only then, later, for security reasons, did he transfer himself to the house of Vlado Santic, from which house he did not leave until UNPROFOR people came at about 15.30 on that same day. He stresses that he had seen Aladin Karahodza in the courtyard of the warehouse, of the Ogrjev plant, waving his hand, and the witness Kujawinski also stated that Aladin Karahodza had come from the courtyard to the road where UNPROFOR vehicles were. In all fairness, he says that he crept and crawled under the wire fence, but this is not correct because it is fastened to the ground, the fence, that is, and there is no room under which to crawl. It falls from the statement of witness Dragan Calic and the photographs which have been presented to this Chamber, as well as from the videotape which was shown, that this wire impediment was, indeed, negotiable, and the mesh is such that it can be surmounted. It follows from the statements of the other witnesses also that this guard post, which had a glazed door and had three windows, one facing east, one west, and the third facing south. According to the videotape which was shown, especially according to the statement of Ivan Brankovic, it follows to the east, that to the east or the warehouse, towards the house of Smail Ahmic and Mujo Ahmic, and let me not list any more houses in that direction. And to the west is the house of Avdo Becirevic. That means that Aladin Karahodza could at any moment leave, without being seen by the guard post and head towards the houses of members of his own ethnic group. In addition to that, it is evident from the statement of Dragan Calic, and was also shown on the videotape, that one can enter the courtyard of the warehouse by two gates; however, one gate was being locked and that was exactly the gate over which Karahodza jumped. However, this is just as if someone were to leave one's house by the chimney rather than by the door. He could have used gate number 1 which has an additional door on the side, so to speak, and it was unlock. He is a young man, 27 years of age, he is not bulky, and he could have evacuated himself from the courtyard when he saw the UNPROFOR vehicles. So the witness is not correct when he contends that he was locked and that he was trembling, because it is not true simply for the reason that both were behaving the same way. The witness said that he had fainted, as also corroborated by Witnesses BB and Witness Z, when the UNPROFOR vehicles came, he lost consciousness out of fear and ended up in the Novi Travnik Hospital. Therefore, the testimony of Witness Z is transparent when he says that Aladin Karahodza was locked in the guard house, interpreting this by the fact that he was in fear, that he was afraid. Finally, we have one peculiarity which runs like a swing throughout this whole case with respect to my client Drago Josipovic, namely here as well as in other cases, the Witness BB was questioned by one of the investigators of the Prosecution, in which case she failed to mention at all Aladin Karahodza. Also, the Witness ZZ was interrogated by the investigators of the Prosecution on the 15th and 17th of November, 1997. It was an extensive interview which took some two days, and on the 2nd of February, 1998, he also gave a statement to the police in Zenica. It was only on the 10th of May in 1998 that he, for the first time, mentioned the case of Aladin Karahodza, which means that the Witness Z and Witness BB, only after the indictment had been disclosed, publicly disclosed and confirmed by the Tribunal, and when Drago Josipovic had already been in The Hague to appear before this Court, it was only then that these -- that this witness locked up Aladin Karahodza in the warehouse of the Ogrijev plant. I also need to mention that in both cases this is a hearsay witness. The question necessarily arises whether this statement can be categorised as admissible evidence. This war story of Aladin Karahodza reminds me of a hunting story, because it is unconvincing, and I do believe that Drago Josipovic, on the night in question, was not at the Ogrijev warehouse, which in itself implies that he had not locked up Aladin Karahodza and could not have threatened him with a pistol. I also have to add to this that the claim of the Prosecutor is also not correct when he says the house of the Drago Josipovic is in the immediate vicinity of Ogrijev. The house of Drago Josipovic is not there. It is a courtyard between his house and the road, and the gun house of the Ogrijev Enterprise is on quite the opposite side of the yard, which means that the house of Drago Josipovic is over a hundred metres away from the guard post and from the scene of the event, which is quite visible on the videotape. So this distance, that is of over a hundred metres. So that Aladin Karahodza could not have been afraid of Drago Josipovic seeing him from Josipovic's house as he crossed over from the other side from the Ogrijev yard to the other side of the road. I'd now like to talk about the count which refers to the murder of Muzafer Puscul, the burning of his house, and the taking away of his family. I should like to stress at the outset that Drago Josipovic has not committed the crime that he's charged with in the indictment, that he had no intention nor no knowledge of the murder of Muzafer Puscul, according to Article 7 of the Statute. The statement of the Witness EE is problematic and wholly unconvincing. She has changed her statements on a number of occasions, and her statement has contradicted her earlier statements, as well as contradictory to the statements of other witnesses who have been questioned before this Trial Chamber. I should proceed by just briefly touching upon the most salient differences in respect to her statement given here before the Trial Chamber vis-à-vis the earlier given statements. Let me just, by way of illustration, mention one sentence, that this witness charges that Drago Josipovic, together with Vladimir Santic and a group of soldiers, burned their house, killed Muzafer Puscul, forcibly abducted them and took them away from their house. So thus the Witness EE, at a hearing on the 8th of October, 1998, said that she could recognise Vlado Santic, Zeljo Livancic, Drago Josipovic, Marinko Katava, Karla Cerkez -- Karlo Cerkez in a matter of two seconds, and somewhat later she also referred to Stipo Alilovic. However, according to the statement of May 14, 1993 which she gave to the public security centre in Zenica, she emphasised that Stipo Alilovic, Zeljo Livancic, Vlado Santic, and Drago Josipovic were the people who were in front of her door. She at that time did not mention Karlo Cerkez or Marinko Katava. According to the statements of the same witness on September 20, 1993, which she gave before the High Court in Zenica, she claimed that she had seen Stipo Alilovic, Zeljko Livancic, Zarko Kristo, and Karlo Cerkez in addition to Drago Josipovic and Vlado Santic. According to a statement on the 1st of February, 1995, which she gave before the investigator of the Prosecutor, she had ostensibly seen Marinko Katava, Zeljo Livancic, Karlo Cerkez -- sorry, Karlo Cerkez, Valdo Josipovic and does not mention Vlado Santic this time. In statements given on the 31st of July, 1996 and the 1st of August, 1996 to the investigator of the Prosecutor, she says that she saw Stipo Alilovic, Vlado Santic, Drago Josipovic, Marinko Katava, Karlo Cerkez, and Zeljo Livancic. The Witness EE is also neither consistent when she describes the persons who killed her husband Muzafer. So on the 8th of October, 1998, she said that it was Vlado -- Zeljo Livancic and Santic that took her husband away. In a statement of the 14th of May, in Zenica, she said it was Stipo Alilovic who had ordered Zeljo Livancic to take away Muzafer, and that Zeljo Livancic did take him behind the shed and after that she could hear bursts of fire. According to the statement that she made to the Higher Court in Zenica, it may be concluded that -- sorry. I stand corrected. According to the statement that she made to the Prosecutor's investigator in February 1995, is it may be concluded that Zeljo Livancic, Vlado Santic, Drago Josipovic, Marinko Katava, took Muzafer Puscul behind the shed. And in the statement that she gave to the Prosecutor's investigator on -- in July 1996 and on the 1st of August, 1996, it seems that Muzafer was taken by Zeljo Livancic and Vlado Santic behind the shed. Mr. President, I am not going to enumerate all these differences any longer, and there are quite a few of them at that. So I shall mention the case of Marinko Katava. The Prosecutor had put forth a proposal to withdraw indictment against Marinko Katava. This was confirmed by the Court. This is meaningful for two reasons. That is to say that Witness EE's testimony is not truthful; and secondly, that the Honourable Trial Chamber does not believe this witness. I should like to mention, in passing, a question. Can a person be convicted on the basis of the testimony of one sole witness? This is a very troublesome issue, and I believe that in this particular case, on the basis of the statement made by one witness only, a sentence cannot be passed. There are several versions of this statement of this witness. She mentioned several different persons on several different occasions, and that is why a judgement of guilty cannot be based on her testimony. I wish to add that the witness's testimony, Witness EE's testimony, is not corroborated by any other evidence. The events by Muzafer Puscul's house cannot be viewed separately by the events that occurred near Nazif Ahmic's house, Azim Ahmic's house, and Ramiz Ahmic's house. This has to be viewed as one whole and in terms of continuous time. Witness DD said that on the 16th of April, 1993, she was awakened in the early morning hours by an explosion. She stresses that from her window she saw a group of soldiers who were coming from the direction of Azim's house; that is to say she saw them by is Azim Ahmic's house, meaning that that group of soldiers was moving from the direction of Muzafer Ahmic's house. That direction of movement was confirmed by Witness FF as well, who also saw a group of soldiers moving from that direction. And the statement of Josip Vidovic speaks in that direction as well; namely, Josip Vidovic said that this was what he was told by Alma, the daughter of Witness DD. The statement of this witness, in relation to the statement of Witness EE, has a single point in common. Both are direct; namely, Witness EE said that a group of soldiers was shooting at her house and torching her house, and while they were still doing that, they set off for Ramiz Ahmic's and Azim Ahmic's house. This is corroborated by witness statements; that is to say, the statements of FF, Josip Vidovic, and Witness DD. I have to mention another question that the Prosecutor avoided. Witness CA said that as she was leaving her own house, she was moving in the direction of Muzafer Puscul's house or, rather, Zarko Kristo's house. Those two houses are near one another. Witness CA testified that in Zarko Kristo's house she saw Karlo Cerkez shooting with a rifle. That testimony coincides with that of Witness EE, who said that her house was being shot at from Zarko Kristo's house for a second time, when her house had already been torched. The distance involved -- that to say from that house to the house of Anto Papic -- is about 700 metres, in my estimate. Witness CA set out with her family towards the house of Nikola Omazic and further on towards the house of Nikola Papic. According to the testimony of this witness, as well as that of Witness BB, it may be concluded that they were walking down a field from Zarko Kristo's house towards the house of Nikola Omazic, and that's where they encountered Drago Josipovic and Witness D. These points forcefully show that Drago Josipovic was not by Muzafer Puscul's house or by Nazif Ahmic's house. The testimony of Witness EE is highly regarded by the Prosecutor. He says that it is reliable, confidential, truthful, and I claim the opposite. When Witness EE described Drago Josipovic, and when Witness DD described Drago Josipovic, there was quite a difference. It would actually seem that it is not the same person concerned. It is not the same Drago Josipovic that is described by Witness EE and Witness DD respectively. Witness DD says that she saw Drago Josipovic from her house as he was coming from the direction of Azim Ahmic's house and shooting. She saw him for a second time, she said, when he was behind her house. He came there after her son Amir had been taken away in the same direction. Witness DD says that Drago Josipovic had a black cap, a black knitted cap, and that he had pulled it over his face. However, I don't blame the Prosecutor for not having noted this difference, because he could not have; namely, the transcript says that Witness EE described Drago Josipovic as having had a multicoloured cap and a visor cap, whereas the other witness said that he had a black knitted cap. I checked with the tape that I got from the Registry here, and I established that Witness EE gave a description of the cap and of Drago Josipovic. However, regrettably this does not enter the transcript. I believe that neither statement is truthful or correct, because other witnesses, for example, Witness CA and Witness CB -- I'm a bit confused. Mr. President, I paused for a while but I shall correct myself because I remembered what I wanted to say. Witnesses CB and CA, respectively, speak differently in relation to the Court witnesses; namely, CB and CA. Namely, both witnesses said that Drago Josipovic, on that morning when they saw him before 6.00, did not have any cap on his head. This is yet another addition and another corroboration to the thesis that Drago Josipovic was not by Muzafer Puscul's house or Nazif Ahmic's house. During the commission of the crimes mentioned in the indictment, Drago Josipovic was at Nikola Omazic's house and that is what Witness DG's statement confirms as well. He said that Drago Josipovic passed by his yard in the morning at 5.15. After a brief conversation, they heard shooting and came to a crossroads where Anto Bralo's house was. After this shooting, they continued towards Nikola Omazic's house and that's where they encountered the families of Witness CA and CB. An event that can be reconstructed on the basis of the testimony of this witness corresponds to the statements of Kovac Katica, Kovac Franjo, Anto Bralo, and Finka Bralo. In the same way they pointed out that on the road by Nikola Omazic's house they saw Drago Josipovic and Witness DG. They also mentioned that they met Witness CA, Witness CB and their families. Witness CA and Witness CB pointed out that they had besieged Drago Josipovic that they seek shelter there, and Drago Josipovic accepted that, especially Witness DG, because CB's children were barefoot and hardly had any clothes on. Witness CB points out in his statement that the children of Witness CB asked them to take them to the house of Witness DG, and then that is what Witness CA asked as well. This is corroborated by Witness CB's statement. She clearly indicated that Witness CA asked Witness DG to take them to their -- to his house. That is to say that when one looks at the inter-relationship between these statements, one can see that they are mutually connected, and they are conducive to the only possible conclusion; that is that in the morning, before 5.30, Drago Josipovic was by Witness DG's house, and near Nikola Omazic's house he encountered the family of Witness CA. I have to particularly highlight the importance of Witness CB's statement. She made a statement to the Prosecutor's investigator and pointed out that she went out of her house five minutes after Fahran Ahmic had been killed. They were in a hurry because the children did not even have time to put their shoes on. She pointed out that by -- that from her house to Witness DG's house, and in the direction from her house towards Muzafer Puscul's house, the visibility was good. The houses are scattered. They are in fields and there was no vegetation at the time. The witness claimed that Drago Josipovic could not have killed her husband and could not have been in the house, which means that he was not by Muzafer Puscul's house either. In her testimony, she stated here, before the Trial Chamber, that a group of soldiers attacked her, and when she left the house, Fahran Ahmic was killed. She did not think, she was in a hurry with her children, and with Witness CA, she set out for Rovna, in the direction of Rovna. She pointed out that it was impossible for her not to see a person moving in that area and claimed that if someone were to be moving in that area, she would have had to see him. The statements of Court Witnesses CA and CB clearly point to the conclusion that Drago Josipovic could not have been by Naser Ahmic's or Muzafer Puscul's house. When Witness DG testified here before the Trial Chamber, he said that the house of Cazim Ramic was right by the road where Drago Josipovic and Witness DG were walking. The house of Cazim Ramic was lit, and there was light in the windows, it's only five metres away from the road, but the house of Mujo Ahmic, where Cazim Ramic happened to be with his family later, as well as Mirsad Osmancevic, is also near the road and it also has windows. During the trial, Witness DG had Cazim Ramic's statement read out to him. The Prosecutor did not oppose that, and according to the statement of Cazim Ramic, it -- I'm sorry. It seems that Drago Josipovic and Witness DG did not kill anyone. He said that the killings were committed by those who were masked. Although I respect the ruling of the Tribunal that this will not be admitted into evidence, I believe that this is an important circumstance. I'm sorry. Witnesses CB and CA, Frano Kovac, Anto Bralo, and Witness DG are, indeed, relevant. That the testimony of Witness EE, when she said that she saw a group of soldiers moving in the direction of Nazif Ahmic's house, is true, is confirmed by the testimony of Witness DH, who said that, from Muzafer Ahmic's barn, you could see the road and the houses of Ramiz Ahmic and Nazif Ahmic. Witness EE stated that she heard voices around Ramiz Ahmic's house, that she heard his voice and the voice of Witness DD. This indicates that the group of soldiers in the house of Witness EE left in the direction of Witness DD's house. Witness FF said that, after the explosion and after she was attacked by members of the army, half an hour elapsed before they left the area, crossed the road, and set out in the direction of Ogrjev. Witness Z, who said that in the night of the 15th to the 16th he spent the night at his house, which is only some 15 metres away from the house, saw early in the morning a group of soldiers crossing the road and going to the northern part of Zume. If the testimony of Witness FF is compared to this, and the length of time she spent in her house and barn, if this is compared to the testimony of Witnesses CA, CB, and DG, we can see two things: First of all, that Drago Josipovic was not in the group which was in EE's house and DD's house and later crossed the road; and if we make a connection between this and the testimony of Zoran Covic, then it is quite clear because he said that he had heard from his father that Ramiz Ahmic's family and Nazif Ahmic's family remained in their houses. So he received this information from someone who knew this. The most intense gunfire was around the road, and no one crossed the road from the direction of DG's house or came back that way. This means that Zoran Covic heard this information from someone who had participated in these events. This again leads to the conclusion that Drago Josipovic was at his home and not in the houses of Muzafer Puscul and Nazif Ahmic. I have already said that, during the first conflict, Drago Josipovic was at his house, and it has been confirmed that the Prosecutor's contention that he was mobilised at that time is incorrect. He was not mobilised on the 16th of April, 1993 either. He was at his home, and this follows from the testimony of Witnesses CA, CB, DG, Frano Kovac, Anto Bralo, Finka Bralo, and Katica Kovac. Exhibit P3, to which the Prosecutor refers, is incorrect in relation to Drago Josipovic because these lists were drawn up so that people could be issued with shares, as many witnesses have said, including Katica Kovac and Vlado Alilovic. Dragan Stojak, who was an employee in the Vitez defence office, said that mobilisation was carried out in the afternoon of the 16th of April, and Vlado Alilovic said that mobilisation was carried out from the 16th to the 28th of April, but step by step, and that it was impossible to establish who was mobilised when. Since Drago Josipovic was at home during this time, this fact leads to the conclusion that he was not an active member of the HVO and that he was not mobilised on the 16th. He was mobilised only on the 19th of April, 1993. This is borne out by the testimony of Anto Bralo, Frano Kovac, and Katica Kovac. With respect to Anto Bralo and Frano Kovac, the documents of the Prosecution also indicate that they were mobilised, which is not correct. Anto Bralo has documents which have been adduced into evidence that he was employed at the British Battalion of UNPROFOR. This excludes the possibility of his having been mobilised, as the Prosecutor claims. Frano Kovac was also not mobilised, and this was established on the basis of his employment booklet. He was employed in Novi Travnik and only came to Santici from time to time. His house was under construction. He did not know the neighbourhood very well, no one knew about him. All of them, together with Drago Josipovic, were mobilised on the 19th of April, 1993. It must be pointed out that Frano Kovac and Anto Bralo, during the first conflict, were at their homes, just like Drago Josipovic. Anto Bralo and Frano Kovac testified that during the first conflict together with Mirsad Osmancevic, they were cutting wood, and the first conflict occurred while they were cutting wood, and so they spent a whole night in the wood. This is further proof of the Defence's claim that neither Anto Bralo, nor Frano Kovac, nor Drago Josipovic were mobilised before the 19th of April, 1993. The Prosecutor claims that Drago Josipovic detained members of the Muslim ethnic group, which is not true. From the testimony of Witness CA, it follows that she asked Drago Josipovic to provide her with a shelter. I have already said that, according to the testimony of Witness CA, who said the same as CB, they asked him to take them into his home. When Witness DG and Drago Josipovic met their families, the children were barefoot and, according to Witness DG, the children asked Witness DG to take them in. Drago Josipovic and Witness DG took them to Witness DG's house, gave them milk, and welcomed them nicely. During the day, Witness CA left the house, as she herself said, and this was corroborated by the testimony of Witness CB. Witness EE also confirmed that she left DG's house. Other witnesses, Katica Kovac, Anto Bralo, and Witness DG all said the same as the aforementioned witnesses; that is, that the house of Witness DG was not locked, that they were able to leave whenever they wanted to. Witness CA went to Fahran Ahmic's house. With regard to Fahran Ahmic's house, it is my opinion that Witness Z's testimony is not correct. He says that in the afternoon of the 16th, when he wasn't feeling well and was getting into a vehicle, happened to notice a group of soldiers in front of Fahran Ahmic's house. The distance is not 20 metres; it's more than 60 metres, and Fahran Ahmic was near that house with a cap. Because Witnesses CA and CB said that on that afternoon, at 15.30 hours, he was at Fahran Ahmic's house, and this is confirmed by the testimony of Witness DH, who said that he, Miro Josipovic, and Nikica Grebenar, went to collect the dead body of Fahran Ahmic, and the fact that Drago Josipovic was not there is borne out by the testimony of Witness CA, who said that she asked Drago Josipovic to go and see the dead body, and he told her that he was afraid and that he could only do it when it started to get dark. So the Prosecutor's allegation that Drago Josipovic was in the courtyard in front of Fahran Ahmic's house is not true. Mirsad Osmancevic is a special case. It should be pointed out that, from the testimony of Witnesses CA and CB, it follows that Witness CA asked Drago Josipovic to bring Mirsad Osmancevic and his family to Witness DG's house, and also Cazim Ahmic, and she repeated her request and asked that Witness EE and her family be brought to Witness DG's house. The Prosecutor is puzzled by the manner in which Drago Josipovic brought these families to that house. It is understandable that Witness CA moved along the road, beside the houses where Cazim Ahmic and Mirsad Osmancevic were, and EE's house is not far away. So they had to be seen. Witness CA is easily recognisable because she wears a headscarf and the Muslim dress, so she and Witness EE and Cazim Ahmic and Mirsad Osmancevic were conspicuous. The Prosecutor is incorrect in saying that Drago Josipovic and Witness DG forcibly locked up Muslims. Mirsad Osmancevic's case shows that this is not so. He had a young baby, and his family, with three small children, went to Rovna. Drago Josipovic helped Mirsad, as his neighbourhood, to go to Rovna. He gave him his vest. But when an HVO soldier threatened to blow up the owner of the house, to blow up the house if he remained there, he came back to DG's house, and this shows that all Muslims could go in and out of that house as they wished. I have to point out that Drago Josipovic and Witness DG saved the wives and children of Muslims, but also able-bodied men, such as Amir Ramiz and Zenur, but Mirsad Osmancevic, who was an officer of the army of B and H, did something wonderful for them at the risk of his own life. As regards the taking away of Muslims from Anto Papic's house, toward Miso Livancic's house, I think that Drago Josipovic did not participate in this at all. Witness EE said that Witness DG came to their house and said that they should go toward the road and that UNPROFOR would take charge of them. Witness CB said that only Witness DG took her there, and Witnesses CB and CA said that, on that occasion, they saw Drago Josipovic in his courtyard, and that they could come and go as they pleased is also corroborated by the witness who said that she crossed the fields towards Fahran Ahmic's house and arrived before the others, who were taking the long way around, and saw Drago Josipovic in the courtyard. But Witnesses DG, Katica Kovac, Finka Bralo, and Anto Bralo said that Drago Josipovic went to his house an hour before Anto Papic took the Muslims to the road and then to Miso Livancic's house. From the testimony of Witnesses EE, CA, and CB, it follows that they then went to Miso Livancic's house, and from the testimony of Witness DG, it follows that he took them there of his own accord. Drago Josipovic did not participate in or omit to do anything he should have when the Muslims were taken toward the road, because it was Witness DG who talked to the representatives of UNPROFOR in German, and when UNPROFOR rejected the Muslims, he himself took them to Miso Livancic's house of his own volition, and throughout this time, Drago Josipovic remained at home. He was later asked by Witness CA whether she could stay, and he said she could, but as he explained, certain things could happen, and this was true. I have already mentioned the testimony of the peculiarities in the testimony of the Prosecution witnesses. Witness DD was questioned by the Prosecutors and investigators on several occasions, and it was only after the indictment was published that she mentioned the case of Drago Josipovic. However, I should also mention the official note of Prosecutor Terrier. I trust him and I also trust his investigator. In the official note, it says that, on the 16th of April, 1993, one of the soldiers threw down a woman who was injured and remained in a coma, and the investigator wrote that Witness EE stated that her son, Amir, was killed by Anto Bralo. If all the other evidence is compared with this note, which has been adduced into evidence, and it was written by the Prosecutor, then the credibility and truthfulness of Witness DD is very questionable. It is claimed that Witness DG said to Witness CB that he himself did not feel very safe in his own house. So Witness DG, who is an elderly person and not in good health and without a very good memory, and the Defence mentioned this problem in the examination, I am pointing this out because the Prosecutor paid the most attention to this witness. Therefore, I consider that Drago Josipovic did not omit to do anything and did not do anything to deserve being charged with persecution and murder. There is nothing to show that he discriminated against Muslims either on ethnic or religious or other grounds. He did not participate in a systematic attack on the Muslims or on individuals. He did not perpetrate a criminal act or in any way participate in or aid and abet the commission of a criminal act. He did not incite others to commit criminal acts. He did not contribute to the commission of other crimes, and there is nothing that would lead to the conclusion that he had the intention of committing a crime. The fact that he had a rifle and a uniform, I repeat, does not mean that he committed any kind of crime. I forgot to mention Witness DG's fear. According to the testimony of Finka Bralo, everyone was afraid when Mirsad Omazic, as an officer of the army of BH, came back to DG's house. There was panic. One should understand that Witness DG was terrified and that he told Witness CB that he was afraid for his own safety and that of his family. It follows from all this that Drago Josipovic did not commit any of the crimes with which he's charged in the amended indictment and, therefore, I propose that he be acquitted by this Court. I also propose that the Court should provisionally release Drago Josipovic, because he volunteered to come to this Tribunal, and Their Honours trusted him and allowed him to attend his mother's funeral and he justified this trust by coming back, and the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina guarantee that they will hand over Drago Josipovic should he fail to come back voluntarily. Your Honours, I have completed my final statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you so much. We now stand adjourned until 11.20. So only 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Before I call upon Counsel Puliselic, I would like to say that we have carefully considered the question of confidentiality of two documents which have been filed, by the Prosecutor the brief, Prosecutor's brief, and the brief filed by Counsel Krajina, and we have decided that these two documents should not be treated as confidential any longer. So they're public documents now. Counsel Puliselic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in its closing argument, the Defence will first of all give a few introductory remarks; touch briefly upon the first and the second conflicts; and then it shall, in polemicising with the final closing argument of the Prosecution, analyse the statements of certain witness -- Defence and Prosecution witnesses. The content of the closing arguments of the Defence shall in principle not be repeated, nor shall we be repeating things that the Defence has already discussed before this Court. In the introduction, the Defence wishes to stress that by the initially brought charges against our client in 1995, which was signed by Prosecutor Goldstone, Dragan Papic had been charged for six criminal offences under Article 2 and Article 3 of the Tribunal's Statute, and according to that indictment for alleged crimes, he predominantly committed those, participated in offences in the village of Pirici, whereby the amended indictment from 1995, he was charged with crimes under Article 5(H) of the Tribunal Statute located in Ahmici. This very fact associated with the venue and the manner of the commission of the criminal offence points to the very question of the credibility of the statements of certain witnesses on the basis of whose testimonies and statements the Prosecution first issued the first indictment and then the second amended indictment at the time when Dragan Papic had already been at The Hague. In addition to this, it follows from the statements of the witnesses for the Defence that on the 16th of April, 1993, when the crimes were committed, Dragan Papic was neither in Pirici, nor in Ahmici, but happened to be next to the -- by the River Lasva guarding a bridge as the most ordinary -- as a most ordinary member of the village guards. By the amended indictment, in Count 1 he is charged with a crime against humanity under Article 5(H) of the Statute, which is to say, for persecution on political, racial, or religious grounds. The Defence contends that nothing contained in this charge has been committed by Dragan Papic, nor did Dragan Papic participate in the first clashes in November 1992, nor in the second conflict which took place on the 16th of April 1993, in a way as to aid and abet or personally commit any of the transactions characterised as penal, as criminal behaviour towards the Muslims. And on April 15, 16, 1993, he did not know the scope or the objectives of the conflict. The Defence wishes also to stress that due to the vague wording of the Prosecution, of the indictment, it was only during the actual hearing that the Defence could conclude what actual behaviour and what actual offences Dragan Papic was being charged with. The Defence claims that Dragan Papic did not commit a single of the offences that he is charged with or that -- according to the statements of some of the witnesses, and that his behaviour does not have the weight of criminal acts to be so characterised under Article 5 of the Tribunal's Statue. And this was expounded in more length, in more detail in the Defence's brief, so I will not repeat that here. In view of the fact that under the indictment on the 20th of October, 1992 -- he is charged with a certain behaviour on the 20th of October, 1992 -- the Defence wishes to stress that it follows from the statement of the witnesses of the Prosecution as well, and in particular the witnesses of the Defence, it follows unquestionably that on the 20th of October, 1992, there were no attacks on the civilian Muslim population in Ahmici, Santici, and Pirici with a view to the persecution or banishment or expulsion. The actual cause of this conflict and this is held unquestionable by the Defence, was the roadblock which had been erected on the main road by the Muslims in order to block passage to HVO units headed for Jajce, where they were headed in order to help their units. It is indisputable that there was fighting between the HVO and the Serbian army at the time in the Jajce area and that after several days the Serbs took Jajce. So the armed conflict on the 20th of October, 1992 was an armed conflict between two armies caused by that barricade, and the Croats actually did not participate -- from Ahmici did not participate in it. The Defence also contends that not a single Muslim house was destroyed deliberately in that conflict, except the house of Mehmed Ahmic. The civil population, the civil Muslim population was not expelled and they returned to their houses, and indeed the Croats invited them to come back. Their houses were not looted; they were not destroyed; they remained intact. The house of Mehmed Ahmici was hit, and it was set on fire by missiles, by shells fired by the HVO and not from weapons which ostensibly, according to the claim of Mehmed Ahmic, was fired by Dragan Papic from the forest. The defendant Dragan Papic -- the witness Mehmed Ahmic had a very high position in the SDA party of the Muslims, and he had high functions otherwise. He was not an ordinary citizen, and he had a very important role in the erection of the roadblock. That is why the HVO actually shelled his house, targeted his house. At the insistence of the Defence, Mehmed Ahmic also admitted that he had taken part in the erection of another roadblock which was installed by the Muslims on the road precisely in front of the house of Ivo Papic. This, according to Mehmed Ahmic, happened before the first clashes. That is why some of the Prosecution's witnesses used this fact and changing the time of the erection of this barricade so that it had been installed by Dragan Papic, who ostensibly had been some sort of a commander on that roadblock. I think this is Witness B. One cannot accept the allegations of Mehmed Ahmic that on the 20th of October in 1992, in the early hours of the morning, Dragan Papic shot from an automatic rifle, from the window of the house in which there were sandbags, at Mehmed's house and later also shot from the woods also at his house. Mehmed Ahmic, however, claimed that his house was set on fire by a shell from Hrasno, from where the house had been targeted by the HVO. Pero Papic, Zdenko Rajic, and Zvonimir Santic confirmed that in the early hours of the morning on the 20th of October, 1992, Dragan Papic went -- namely, the clash broke out -- went -- set out for Gornja Rovna with the female part of his family, so to speak, where he met Nenad Santic, the commander of the village guard in Ahmici, and on that occasion Nenad Santic gave him a 60-millimetre mortar with signal flares. And he headed for Donja Rovna, near the house of the witness Santic, with the objective to signalise the possible advance of Muslims from Gornja, Upper Rovna. According to the statement of Santic, the whole time -- throughout this time Dragan Papic, while these clashes around the barricade lasted, he was in the fields until the end of the clash in -- around 4.00 p.m., so that he could not have, at the same time, shot at the house of Mehmed Ahmic from various weapons. From the statement of the expert witness Wagenaar, in view of the fact that the woods from which Dragan Papic allegedly shot is a hundred metres away from the house of Mehmed Ahmic, it follows that Mehmed Ahmic could not at all have recognised Dragan Papic, nor the other persons who he alleges to have seen there. Especially not in a situation when fleeing from his own house, bent over, and carrying his son in his arms. He could also not have seen Dragan Papic at the window in a black uniform -- and he claimed that he had seen him up to the waist -- because at the same time, he also asserted that the sandbags reached half of the height of the window, so that he could only see the head but not the black uniform. But still, even so, he could not have recognised him in view of the testimony given by Professor Wagenaar, because Ahmic claimed that the house of Papic's claimed was 70 metres away from his own. Let me say a few words about the conflict on the 16th of April, 1993. The Prosecutor claims that Dragan Papic helped in the preparations for the April attack in 1993 in a way -- in the way which has been described under paragraph 9 of the amended indictment. Inter alia it mentions military training, refers to military training, and the only military training that Dragan Papic had ever had in his life was the military training that he had during his service in the army, in the former Yugoslav People's Army; which is to say, several years prior to this conflict. During that training, he learned how to use a gun, a M-48, and a 60-millimetre mortar. This was described by Goran Papic, Zdenko Rajic and other witness. I also wish to mention that none of the witnesses of the Prosecution said that Dragan Papic participated in any military training. Dragan Papic had not armed himself in any way whatsoever for -- by way of preparation for the April attack in 1993. He did have an ordinary M-48 rifle that he had been issued by his enterprise where he worked as a game warden, as a woods warden, and he had that gun only since he found that particular job and not before. I believe that it is not at all disputable that Dragan Papic was an employee of the forestry enterprise until the beginning of the war which broke out on the 15th of April, 1993, and to corroborate that the Defence has presented the employment record of the defendant, which has been admitted into evidence. This was also corroborated by both Prosecution and Defence witnesses, that he was a game warden. Precisely because Papic was permanently employed until the war, he participated in a much smaller degree, much less than other people, in the village guard's patrols. The night prior to the conflict, Dragan Papic evacuated his family. This is based, by the Prosecutor, on the statement of Witness A, who said on the 15th of April, 1993, he saw Dragan Papic, in the evening, taking away women, driving away women in a red Lada car. On the other hand, the Witness F, when he was 14 years old, saw a red Lada, which he believes was owned by Dragan Papic, around 3.00 in the afternoon, taking away women and children, but there were no children at that time yet in Dragan Papic's house. I wish to stress that the Witness F never referred to this when speaking to the investigators. The Prosecution -- the Defence refers to the statements of Ankica Vidovic, Goran Papic, who said that at the time Dragan Papic had a Zastava 101 make automobile, popularly called a Stojadin, and it was yellow. In addition to that, the sales contract for the car in question, which is also in the file, shows clearly that Dragan Papic did have a red car of Lada make, but it happened only 1995, not during the -- in the time of the conflict, that is. After that, the witness Ljubica Milicevic, Zoran Santic, and Goran Papic saw Dragan Papic leading on foot the female part of his family, on the 16th of April, 1993, the early morning hours after the shooting had already started. In fact, Dragan Papic was fleeing, escaping after the shooting broke out, so as to find shelter for his pregnant, nine-months-gone wife, and for his mother and his sister, and they headed for Gornja Rovna where it was calmer and more peaceful. As his wife was pregnant and far gone, it's obvious, not only from the statements, but also from the documents about the birth of his son Marijan on the 28th of April, 1993, that the attendant was a Muslim, Ufeta Tuco. This was the person they trusted the most, and she was a Muslim. Had Dragan Papic hated Muslims, he would not have this woman as the birth attendant attending the birth of his son. Witness A says that on the 16th and 17th of April, 1993 he saw a machine gun, some sandbags in the house of Dragan Papic, and on the 17th of April, that he saw Dragan Papic himself wearing a black uniform. In contrast to that witness, the witnesses Ljubica Milicevic, Pero Papic, and Goran Papic claimed that never had there been any weapon in front of the house of Dragan Papic, not a machine gun or anything similar. The witnesses for the Defence also disprove the witnesses for the Prosecution as regards this machine gun and other manner of weapons in front of the house of Dragan Papic prior to the conflict, and it is, in addition to that, illogical that Dragan Papic would have kept by his house -- or made his father's house a military fortification, especially in view of the fact that his wife was about to give birth. This witness could not have seen Dragan Papic by his house on the 17th of April, 1993 because, at that time, he was doing guard duty on Radak Bridge, and, according to the statement of witnesses, he never left the post. The Defence also claims that on the 16th of April, 1993, in the afternoon hours, an UNPROFOR unit entered Ahmici, and at that time, there was a crew filming many of the details of the occurrence, and it has been shown here. Had there existed a machine gun nest in front of Dragan Papic's house, it is certain that the crew would have filmed that, because this house is quite near the road which the UNPROFOR vehicles were on. However, this very significant detail is absent from that footage; that is to say, Witness A is simply not saying the truth. The indictment also claims that Dragan Papic organised HVO soldiers and munitions and weapons. The position of Dragan Papic and his importance in Ahmici in no way enabled him to organise soldiers or weapons or ammunition, or anything else associated with military units. He had no political or military function whatsoever; he only was a soldier. The Prosecution has failed to prove that Dragan Papic prepared his house and his relative's house as a staging area and final location for the attack. First of all, in order to be able to do that, he would have had to know that there was an imminent attack, but he didn't know anything about it. On the 15th of April, 1993, a day prior to the critical day, during the working hours, he was at his work post, and thereafter he was repairing cars, as testified to here by Goran Papic. In addition to that, there was also with him his wife, who was about to give birth, and in such a situation, it would only be an insane man, a lunatic who would give his house for a staging area, or keep weapons and ammunition stored in his house. In addition, there were also another two women in the house, his mother and his sister, and I'm sure it's obvious that they would not have allowed that. This is why we find unacceptable the statements of the witnesses of the Prosecution which charge Dragan Papic so. These witnesses are frustrated people, due to their experience, and they are also under the constant pressure of the Muslim Secret Service. It is highly indicative that numerous witnesses have changed every new statement to the investigator, before the Trial Chamber, and expanded the charges vis-à-vis Dragan Papic with every successive statement. In the early morning hours of the 16th of April, 1993, when the shooting started, most of the Croats started fleeing as well, seeking shelter and taking shelter. Most of the population had no idea either who was attacking, nor what the proportions or the objectives of the attack were. They were all equally frightened and they were all equally ignorant of what was actually going on. Therefore, Dragan Papic could not have concealed from other Muslim inhabitants that an attack was imminent because he was not aware of it himself. The indictment claims that Dragan Papic was an HVO soldier. Dragan Papic became a soldier when he was mobilised, and this mobilisation was carried out starting from the 16th of April, 1993. He got an official summons after his wife gave birth. Therefore, Dragan Papic is the last person on the list of mobilised persons, under number 349. This is Prosecutor's Exhibit P335. The Defence will briefly recall some of the other Prosecution witnesses who indict Dragan Papic. Charles Stevens, only towards the end of the second day of his testimony here in court, recognised Dragan Papic. All of us here in this courtroom remember that moment very well because, after that, the Trial Chamber issued a new ruling in respect of contacts with witnesses by the Defence and the Prosecution. Obviously, he got confused in terms of the person he talked to for the first and last time in Ahmici, mentioning him as Dragan Papic; namely, the mentioned witness, in response to the question put by the Defence, said that he could not recognise Dragan Papic with 100 per cent certainty because the person he communicated with, mostly in sign language, for 20 minutes and who boasted to him of having killed 32 Muslims did not wear a beard; whereas the person he recognised in the courtroom as the person with whom he had contact did have a beard. The Defence proved through D5, and that is a videocassette, as well as through many witness statements, it ascertained that at that time Dragan Papic did wear a beard, not the kind that he had in the courtroom at that time but a big beard, a very noticeable one. It was also mentioned in passing that expert witness Wagenaar stated that to remember a face one had never seen before is hardly possible after six weeks' time, and in the case of Witness Stevens, it is not a six-week period but a six-year period that is in question. On the basis of all of this, and on the basis of the Prosecutor's closing argument, it seems that he still believes this witness because he has no reason not to speak the truth. I wish to recall the first indictment that was issued against Dragan Papic in 1995, when also a witness said before the investigator that he made Muslim prisoners dig trenches in Pirici and that on that occasion, Dragan Papic killed Jusuf Ibrakovic. Obviously, that witness got confused too because the indictment was amended after it was ascertained that the perpetrator was not Dragan Papic but another person. Witness G claims that on the 16th of April, 1993 he saw Dragan Papic with a rifle in his hands, in the presence of two soldiers in front of the house of Husein Ahmic and that the person in question was lying dead on the ground. Although this witness said in his previous statements that Dragan Papic was always wearing a black uniform, now all of a sudden he said that he was wearing a camouflage, with a cap on his head. The Defence wishes to emphasise that this witness is the only Prosecution witness who claims to have seen Dragan Papic on the 16th of April, 1993 in Ahmici. However, as regards this same event, on the 16th of April, 1993, in front of the house of Husein Ahmic, Witnesses E, F, and CC, Prosecution witnesses, gave evidence concerning the same matter, but none of them mentioned Dragan Papic. All of them spoke of soldiers only, although they know Dragan Papic well. So Dragan Papic was recognised only by Witness G, who at the time was only 13 years old, who was terrified, whose family had been killed then, who was in a state of shock, and who had lost consciousness several times on that day because he had been wounded. Witness G seriously indicted Dragan Papic, brought serious charges against him only in 1998. Then finally, the investigator, who was taking the statement, asked him why this was the first time he had spoken about this in this way, although he had given statements previously as well, starting from 1993 onwards. In response to a question put by the Defence, the witness said that he had never mentioned this before because he was afraid of Dragan Papic. This assertion of his is unacceptable because, after the war, he came to Ahmici several times, including Papic's house, offering his land for sale, saying that he wanted to go abroad. Vlatko Kupreskic was also heard as a witness here, and he said that Witness G offered him his land for sale too. Witness G is not a reliable witness, and the most telling proof of this is that he stated that on the 15th of April, 1993, Croat children did not attend school in Ahmici because they all knew in advance what would happen the next day, which is in contradiction with the statement made by Fikreta Vidovic, the teacher, and also the statement of Witness H, who said that all Croat children had been to school that day. Dragan Papic, on the 16th of April, 1993, did not help or support the killing of Muslims. The Defence claims that the established facts prove unequivocally that he was not in Ahmici on that day, he was at Radak's Bridge, and that from there he could not have seen or known what was going on in Ahmici. Ahmici cannot be seen from Radak's Bridge, and Ivo Vidovic gave evidence to that effect. He stood guard with Dragan Papic and said that no one was allowed to leave his guard post, and Dragan Papic was present there throughout. Zvonimir Santic said the identical thing, and he was incessantly on guard on that day and the previous day for 30 hours. In addition, Ljubica Milicevic, a witness, stated that she saw Dragan Papic around the bridge when she went to the spring to fetch some water. Even if Dragan Papic had found out on the next day what had happened in Ahmici, his behaviour could not be qualified as supporting the persecution of Muslims. In the early morning hours of the 16th of April, 1993, shooting started, and Dragan Papic, together with his wife, mother, and sister, fled as fast as he could to Donja Rovna, and he encountered Nenad Santic, who expected him to go that way, and he lived in the neighbourhood as well. As commander of the village guard, he sent him to Radak's Bridge. Nenad Santic at that time was not an HVO soldier and he did not have anything to do with the HVO; he was simply in charge of the village guards, as several witness statements have shown. Nenad Santic, until the war, was employed at the gasoline station in Vitez, as presented by Witness Ivo Vidovic, and later, he was mobilised like everyone else, and he was killed at the front line. In the municipality of Vitez, the HVO did not have any communication whatsoever with the village guards in terms of command, organisation, armament, supervision, et cetera. The situation was quite different in the area of the municipality of Busovaca because the war broke out there in January 1993. Therefore, there was a kind of relationship between the village guards and the HVO, and Zvonimir Santic, a witness, also spoke about this. He was the commander of the village guards in Donja Rovna, and, as we know, Donja Rovna belongs to the municipality of Busovaca. Therefore, this relationship between the HVO and the village guards in the municipality of Busovaca cannot be viewed as an analogy to the municipality of Vitez. The witnesses who testified during the Prosecution case that Dragan Papic was a participant in the persecutions are traumatised persons and victims of the conflict on the 16th of April, 1993. These persons were forced to bury their dead, to leave their destroyed homes, to heal their wounds, to leave Ahmici, where they had been born and where they had lived. Due to all of that, their truth is a partial, subjective truth. Therefore, for the greater part, their testimonies are unacceptable. Again, the Defence wishes to quote Professor Wagenaar, who said that persons who are very emotional cannot be rational in their positions. The witness Abdulah Ahmic, on the basis of his alleged conversation with Dragan Papic, as far back as 1991, concluded that the entire Croatian population was, in his opinion, getting ready to attack the Muslim population, although at that time there were no hints whatsoever that there could be a war between the Croats and the Muslims. The Serbs were the enemies of the Croats, and they waged war against them, not the Muslims. Abdulah Ahmic also claimed here in court that Dragan Papic was in uniform and that he carried a sniper and that precisely on the 20th of October, 1992, from Papic's house, sniper shooting came, in his opinion, when he was 300 metres away. Although he previously talked to the investigators, Ahmic never mentioned that, just like many other details. The Defence believes that this witness was very upset because of the suffering of the members of his family and that, in the courtroom, he talked under the influence of all these events. Also, Mehmed Ahmic testified here in this court that Dragan Papic could not have carried a sniper because he did not have one, and that is what Defence witnesses talked about. Dragan Papic had an ordinary rifle that had been issued to him by his company. Abdulah Ahmic, in response to a question put by the Defence as to how he knew that from a 300-metre distance he was shot at by a sniper, he answered that it must have been a sniper because the targeting was so precise; that is to say, Abdulah Ahmic knows exactly where the shooting came from, he knew that the targeting was very precise, and he therefore believes that it was a sniper, although with all this precision, he had not been hit. What can we say about what Abdulah Ahmic also said, that on one occasion, between the two conflicts, he saw Dragan Papic carrying some kind of a strangling device? It is, indeed, strange how, out of this entire arsenal of weapons, Dragan Papic did not kill anyone or strangle someone with the above-mentioned device. The witness Fahrudin Ahmic, the Prosecutor believes that his testimony is reliable too, although he considerably changed his statement while testifying in court in relation to what he had said to the investigator. Some of the things he told the investigator he never mentioned in the courtroom, and he said that others were a mistake because he had been confused. In the courtroom, he said that, on the 16th of April, 1993, he heard shooting from the house of Dragan Papic, although it is actually the house of Ivo Papic that is concerned. This witness, like all others, knows this very well, but, of course, Dragan Papic had to be mentioned in any context. It is quite incredible that when there is shooting all over the place, the witness can assess that the shooting was coming exactly from Papic's house and that he can hear the shooting coming from Papic's house, although he cannot see it. Later, when he was wounded, he claims that he saw fire from a bullet, and he also noticed two soldiers in front of Papic's house who were bent over. Fahrudin Ahmic claimed to the investigators that he was wounded as he was getting out of the house of Hilmija Ahmic and that it was precisely then that he saw rifle fire from Dragan Papic's house. On the basis of the statement made to the investigator, the Defence made a video from all these positions that were mentioned during that statement and ascertained that from Hilmija's yard, one cannot see Papic's house, only the top of the roof, let alone the yard itself, where this witness claims to have seen two soldiers. The Defence also asserted the reverse; that is to say, that from the windows of Papic's house, one cannot see at all the window in front of Hilmija Ahmic's house because one cannot see it from the other houses, and also from the vegetation; however, Fahrudin Ahmic remembered, or somebody told him, that this filming had been made and that his statement could be double-checked that way, and then in the courtroom, he changed his statement, saying that he was wounded at another place, much further away from Hilmija Ahmic's house where Dragan Papic's house can be seen easily. He also added that the shooting was coming from Mehmed Ahmic's house, and of course no one lived there at the time. Therefore, the Defence proposed that the statement made by Fahrudin Ahmic to the investigators be admitted into evidence so that the Trial Chamber could see how significant the differences are in his different statements. The Defence claims that on the 16th of April, 1993, in the house of Ivo Papic, during the day there were none of the persons who actually lived in that house because everyone left the house that day after the shooting started in the early morning hours. Whether some of the soldiers got into the house or not or were around the house, that is something no member of the Papic family knows. In his final brief, the Prosecutor shows the link between Dragan Papic and the HVO, stating that Dragan Papic allowed his house to be used, as well as his land, on numerous occasions, and that the HVO had a high degree of activity there not only during the first and second conflict but also on other occasions. First of all, the Defence wishes to say that on the basis of witness statements, the Prosecutor in this is misstating that this is Dragan Papic's house. This is the land, forest, and house of Ivo Papic. Ivo Papic lives in this house to the present day, whereas Dragan Papic, in 1995, moved with his family to Vitez. The Papic family is a very patriarchal family and the witnesses of the Prosecution know very well that Ivo Papic is the Lord and master in that house. In addition to that, the forest where the shooting came from is to a lesser extent the property of Ivo Papic and to a greater extent the property of other persons, and even on the assumption that the shooting came from that forest, the question remains whether the owners could have opposed the military units and whether the soldiers would have listened to them and left the forest altogether. What is there to be said about Witness B, on whom the Prosecutor also relies, and who charges Dragan Papic with participating in the guarding of checkpoints and setting up roadblocks, and says that he even commanded a roadblock. With regard to Witness B, the Defence wishes to say that this witness, about the checkpoint which was set up previously, stated that it was set up by the Croats, and he presented Dragan Papic as some kind of commander at that roadblock. Mehmed Ahmic himself, during his testimony, at the insisting of the Defence, later admitted, very reluctantly, that this roadblock was actually set up by the Muslims even before the first clash. It was set up in front of his house and that he himself asked for it to be moved. So it was moved to a place near Dragan Papic's house, but he represented it as having been set up by the Croats between the two clashes and accused Dragan Papic of this although he had nothing to do with it. Who is Witness B? Witness B was, first of all, a professional officer in the JNA. Then he joined the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and was a security officer there. He came to Ahmici very rarely, and now suddenly between the two clashes he says he saw Papic in compromising situations. It is not clear what Witness B was doing in Ahmici at all, since he was an officer in the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina at that time. Should he have not been in the zone of operations or was he ordered to go to Ahmici? This witness and the members of his family have reason to accuse the Croats who lived in Ahmici at the time of the conflict. The Defence wishes to stress that Witness B is the son of Witness KL and the brother of Witness EE. The fact that relatives of this witness suffered, shows quite clearly that they were traumatised, and they are representing what they supposed to have happened as the absolute truth. Several Prosecution witnesses allege to have seen various kinds of weapons in front of his house: a machine gun, an anti-aircraft gun, various kinds of guns, and they all mention different positions. Some say there was sandbags in front of it. Others say there was concrete blocks. Some say that the machine gun nest was on the left side of the house; others say it was on the right side. A third witness says it was 50 metres away from the house and closer to the other houses. Witness D, mentioned by the Prosecutor in his closing brief, who says this witness allegedly saw shooting with incendiary bullets from the direction of Zume, of Radak, but also from Papic's house before the 16th of April 1993, but we may ask what this witness actually saw and heard. The same witness also claimed to have seen Dragan Papic going to the Bungalow, but to a question put by the Defence, she finally answered that she did not actually see this but only supposed he had gone there because there was nowhere else for him to go. In his closing brief, the Prosecutor claims that HVO records show that Dragan Papic was part of a battalion in Novi Travnik, from the 22nd of February, 1993, as a courier, but this is contrary to the claims that he held an important post, because to be a courier is the least important post one can hold. This is contrary to the testimony of Witness B, to the list of people in Vitez, according to which Dragan Papic was the member of -- was a member of a regiment in Vitez, home guard regiment in Vitez, and this data demonstrates the questionable nature of much of the evidence presented by the Prosecution, especially as regards Exhibit B351. This list includes many names for women, elderly men, even Muslims, including the Muslim midwife who attended Papic's wife, and the Defence has demonstrated that this list was drawn up for the purpose of issuing shares and there was no home guard regiment at all. It did not exist at that time. But I will not going into this because my colleague has already spoken about it. In his closing brief, the Prosecutor mentions mobilisation during a certain period of time, and Dragan Papic was a reservist and could not have been an HVO soldier. In his closing brief, the Prosecutor claims that Defence witnesses are unreliable, and although the Prosecutor does not deny that Dragan Papic guarded Radak's bridge for a time, he says that he was not there all the time, and he doubts witness Ivo Vidovic because he said that he did not know that the village guards were involved in the conflict of the 20th of October, 1992. Dragan Papic had his work, and he was busy with his work day and night, and he could not know -- was Ivo Papic supposed to know about agreements between the Croats or Muslims or the names of certain units. There are simply people who are not interested in such matters, just as there are others who are but are not interested in something else. Furthermore, Ivo Vidovic did not deny that many Muslims were killed in Ahmici, as the Prosecutor says, but he only said that he learned about the extent of this as time went by, gradually, and not in the beginning while he was standing guard at Radak's bridge. The Prosecutor also doubts the testimony of Zvonimir Santic, who was standing guard on the other side of the bridge, although he -- because he was able to say who was standing guard on one side of the bridge but not on the other. However, there is a logical explanation for this, because there were only two persons standing guard on one side and many more of them on the other side.
