At least ten people were involved and they took turns, but Zvonimir Santic, as the commander, was there most often. So there is nothing strange in the fact that he does not remember who was with him at any given moment. The Prosecutor also doubts the testimony of Goran Papic, and the Prosecutor believes that only Prosecution witnesses are telling the truth, although, there are many parts of their testimony that are illogical, that do not correspond to each other. I would like to mention that Defence witnesses also mention a 60-millimetre mortar which Dragan Papic had. I would like to say that none of the Prosecution witnesses mentioned this weapon. Had Defence witnesses been unreliable, they would not have mentioned this weapon, which was used by the Prosecution later on to incriminate him. He learned to use this weapon in the JNA, just as he learned to handle a M-48 rifle, and it is because of this that Nenad Santic gave Dragan Papic this mortar. The testimony of witness Ljubica Milicevic is also unreliable as is the testimony with Zdenko Rajic, but I do not have time to elaborate on this. The Prosecutor does not believe that Dragan Papic, before the gunfire broke out on the 16th of April, 1993, did not know that there was to be an attack on Ahmici, because Dragan Vidovic said a meeting was held in Jozo Livancic's house on that morning where it was concluded that the members of the village guard should tell everybody else that there was going to be an attack and they should evacuate their families on time. This shows that Dragan Papic was not a regular member of the village guard, and no one informed Papic's family about the imminent attack because they thought that this family that was in the lower part of the village would be able to go to Donja Rovna easily and that it was more important to inform the inhabitants of the middle and upper part of the village. The Prosecutor does not deny that before the war Dragan Papic was on good terms with Muslims, but referring to the expert witness Tone Bringa, he says that due to the mounting tension and hostilities, these relations changed in character. However, the Defence says that it is not only the Croats but also the Muslims who changed because mounting tension and hostilities cannot change the character of only one side and not the other. That is why a number of witnesses tried to lay as much as possible on Dragan Papic, even things that are absurd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Puliselic, your time is up. I wonder if you could wrap up in one or two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will. The Prosecutor mentioned that there were no extenuating circumstances in favour of the accused because they did not cooperate with the Prosecution. The Defence considers that cooperation with the Prosecution is not the only extenuating circumstance that should be taken into account. The courts in the former Yugoslavia would have seen the fact that Dragan Papic gave himself up voluntarily as an extenuating circumstance, after he learned that an indictment had been raised against him. Furthermore, he has family and small children, and his wife is unemployed. This is also an extenuating circumstance. Another extenuating circumstance is the fact that Dragan Papic has no previous criminal record, and he never had any problems with the law. Finally, it should be borne in mind that in detention, where he has been for over two years, he behaved well and was disciplined and did not come into conflict with anyone, which the Court can easily check. The Defence considers that the evidence presented by the Prosecution does not show reliably that Dragan Papic contributed to a policy of persecution as the Prosecutor claims, because Dragan Papic did not know that there was an alleged policy of persecution of Muslims, nor was he in Ahmici on the day that the crime occurred. The Defence proposes that the Court accept the facts put forward in the final brief of the Defence and acquit Dragan Papic fully. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we adjourn, let me rectify our previous ruling about confidential documents. I mentioned only in addition to the final brief by the Prosecutor the closing briefs by Counsel Krajina, but I realise that also other briefs were filed confidentially, the one by Counsel Slokovic-Glumac, Counsel Radovic, and Counsel Susak. Of course, what we decided before also applies to this and other closing briefs. They all will be treated as non-confidential and so they will become public documents. We will adjourn now for ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Before calling upon Counsel Pavkovic, let me say that we have decided to deny the motion orally filed by Counsel Susak concerning the provisional release of Mr. Josipovic, and this is for the same reasons as those mentioned before and concerning the other three motions for provisional release. Counsel Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, Your Honours, in this final moment of this rather exhaustive and long debate, I'm fully convinced that in your minds, the conviction has already prevailed as to the decision to be brought in respect of Vladimir Santic. Numerous witnesses have been heard on both sides, experts have been heard who have helped us jurists resolve some dilemmas which fall outside our own professional competence, you have seen numerous exhibits and pieces of evidence, and is your conviction that the defendant Vladimir Santic is guilty or innocent? I'm certain that this second conviction has prevailed in your minds that Vladimir Santic is not guilty as charged under any of the counts of the indictment, and if that is indeed so, my task at this particular moment is, indeed, a modest one. I shall only, on the basis of a sober assessment of all the evidence presented, point to the reasons wherefore you, Your Honours, could pronounce Vladimir Santic not guilty with a very peaceful conscience. In its closing arguments and closing brief, the Prosecution, very knowledgeably recalling the tragic events of the 16th of April, 1993, aroused emotions towards which no one can be indifferent, neither then nor now. After all these witnesses have passed through the court chamber, no one can remain indifferent to crime, if not directly affected by it. I am convinced that this Trial Chamber will preserve judiciousness and only weigh the proved facts, as is indeed incumbent upon you by your conscience and by your honour as Judges. My distinguished colleagues, counsel for the Defence, prior to my own exposition, have already discussed a number of issues which have to do with the defence for Vladimir Santic, and I shall not repeat those. I support their positions, especially the positions of my learned colleague Susak, because, by the indictment, the Prosecution charged both his and my defendant for the same offences. The only thing which I do have to notice and say about the fact that the defence of Vladimir Santic does not subscribe to that is by my learned colleague Slokovic, and I quote, she said, "The complete unit of the military police participated in the attack on Ahmici." I am convinced that this was a slip of the tongue; however, even if that were not so -- and it is -- I will warn when the right moment comes, I'll point to some considerations which highly bring this proposition into question. It is not just a matter of statements by witnesses but it's a matter of material proof which will prove, in a most reliable way, that this was a statement which was incorrect. The statement I'm referring to is "The complete unit ..." the whole unit, "... of the military police participated ..." At this point, I should like to say a few words about the amended indictment and the actual charges in that indictment against my client, Vladimir Santic. To remind you, the Prosecutor charges Vladimir Santic with a crime against humanity, persecution on religious and national grounds, and expounds in more detail his charges in paragraphs 9, 10, 20, and 21, but basically, his charges could be summed up as follows: The defendant, in union with others, defendants, of course, with other -- some of them defendants -- members of the HVO, being a soldier, participated in the attack on Ahmici on the 16th of April, 1993. It was the intention, as the Prosecutor claims, to cleanse the Bosnian Muslims from that area, and in pursuance of that intention, the defendant undertook actions to deliberately persecute the Muslims and bring about their destruction on a wide scale. The Prosecutor also charged Vladimir Santic with violation of the laws or customs of war, which offence he legally characterised as murders or cruel treatment. Before I start to analyse the thesis of the Prosecutor, I should like to point out to Your Honours a peculiar characteristic which I should like to ask you to bear in mind, hoping that it certainly deserves your attention; namely, in his amended indictment, the Prosecutor has charged Vladimir Santic exclusively as an HVO soldier, and everything that he alleges in that indictment was based, by the Prosecutor, on that particular position or those particular grounds, the defendant being an HVO soldier. However, in his closing brief, and particularly in his closing oral presentation, the Prosecutor concentrated all of his thesis in order to prove that he was primarily responsible for having commanded his inferiors to undertake persecution actions in Ahmici on the relevant dates. He says that my client had a commanding role in the military police, that he was a commander and that he conveyed orders, which he supplemented with his own orders, that he conveyed orders from the superiors, and he held the duty of commander and issued commands and orders. This is, for the first time, in contravention of the confirmed indictment, and despite it, where he was treated only as an HVO soldier, in this argument, he was placed in the role of a commander and the commanding officer, and it is upon those grounds that the Prosecutor actually constructed his culpability. The Defence is deeply troubled by this way of proceeding and wonders then what is the sense of the confirming of the indictment by the Court if the Prosecutor is able, of his own will, to thus change the Rules of Procedure? Does this not then call into question the fairness principle, not to mention the dilemmas that the Defence was faced with? Does the accused have the right to defend himself only against the charges that have been alleged against to him, or can there be some new ones? The Prosecutor will even object to the Defence that it failed to provide evidence with respect to the fact that the defendant was the commander of the 1st Company of the military police in the relevant place, and that is paragraph 1061 on pages 222 and on. In all fairness, formally observed, the Prosecutor will refer to, will invoke Article 7, paragraph 1 of the Statute, but in terms of the substance of his claim, it will be possible to conclude that he is, in fact, charging Vladimir Santic under paragraph 3 of that article, because he says, in his closing brief, the responsibility arises from his omission or failure to punish his inferiors for the crimes committed by them. I felt the need, Your Honours, to point to this particular consideration, and it is for you to evaluate the relevance of this. I do feel that it is relevant, and I shall adduce my reasons for this opinion because that is actually the basic thread of this line of defence. In my further exposition, I will deal with the Prosecution's argumentation whereby he corroborated or, rather, sought to corroborate his charges as legitimate, and then I shall try to explain what would have happened had the Prosecutor charged the defendant on these grounds, which he actually did do in this final portion of the proceedings, in order to prove that in that case, the defendant Vlado Santic is in no way associated with the events in Ahmici on the 16th of April, 1993, and particularly not in the way propounded by the Prosecution. The amended indictment on persecution based on religious and national grounds, in order to prove his thesis of the persecution of the Bosnian Muslims, the Prosecution summoned several witnesses to this court, and they have given testimony in this chamber. In all fairness, the Defence did not know and was unable to find out, in some situations did not know what witnesses the Prosecution was trying to use in order to corroborate its claims that the defendant had indeed committed those offences. I, as the Defence counsel, needless to say, concentrated not only on the thesis but the argumentation to be used to corroborate that claim. Accordingly, I decided to take under consideration all the testimonies of all witnesses who mentioned Vladimir Santic at all in their statements, and after an evaluation of all these statements, of all these testimonies, I concluded that the Prosecutor has failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant Vladimir Santic had directly participated in the events in Ahmici on the 16th of April, 1993, nor had he been associated with those events, involved in those events in any way whatsoever; rather, the defendant, and I will prove and show that later, just happened to be there when the events in question took place, and I shall explain that in more detail during the further course of my statement. Thus, the -- in order to support his claims, the Prosecutor summoned Witnesses B, AA, Sulejman Kavazovic, Zaim Kablar, Lee Whitworth, and Witness EE. If we exclude Witness EE, and we do have to exclude this witness at this particular point because I will be devoting special attention to Witness EE, because it is on the testimony of that witness that the Prosecutor grounds another of his theses in the indictment. So if we leave that witness aside for the time being, and that is the only witness who claims that on the 16th of April Vlado Santic had been in Ahmici, I then wonder what the other witnesses invited by the Prosecutor are saying in their statements. Witness B. He, as the Defence perceives, should have served for the Prosecution to prove that immediately prior to this conflict, the defendant had some sort of an association with the unit which, according to the Prosecution, directly participated in the conflict in question. According to the statement of this witness, Santic, on the night -- on the eve of the attack, was seen in the Bungalow where he allegedly conveyed certain orders. The fact that this is a hearsay witness is not what I'm invoking as an argument in order to object to the credibility of his statement. What it is is that it is an unreliable statement because it is grounded on the unreliable facts; namely, that witness did not have full insight into the actual state of affairs; namely, the witness said that in Stari Vitez he was present when a young HVO prisoner was being questioned, which prisoner had allegedly said, having been a member of the HVO, that one evening Vladimir Santic came to the Bungalow and conveyed these orders. First of all, this witness, according to his own admission, was not present throughout the questioning of that witness. Secondly, this young soldier, the prisoner, never returned after having been imprisoned. Thirdly, and most importantly, when the witness claimed that this questioning was carried out in accordance with the Geneva Conventions on the treatment of prisoners, it would be expected that there is some kind of a written record of that. I wish to recall that in response to your question, Mr. President, as to whether there was any trace of that, whether there was a record of that, the Prosecution answered that there was not, that there was no record. That is why I bring into question everything this witness said. And I believe that this witness's statement cannot be the basis for any kind of conclusion that Vlado Santic was in the place where this witness said he was and that Vlado Santic uttered the words that the witness asserted he uttered. I also have to reiterate what my colleague Mr. Puliselic said; that is to say, that Witness EE's brother is the other witness mentioned, but that is something that I will go back to later. Witness AA. When we see how much time the Prosecutor devoted to this witness's questioning, including the statement he made before trial, we can conclude that this is a very important witness for the Prosecutor and that is the way he was treated during the proceedings. This seems to be a relevant witness, therefore. The information proffered by this witness were many-fold. He belonged to the military police and, therefore, the Prosecutor believes that he had at his disposal such information that he could corroborate his thesis about the role of Vlado Santic. However, all these statements that he made should actually be categorised as statements related to relevant facts pertaining to the persecution of Bosnian Muslims, because Witness EE is a Muslim. Also, those theses which speak about the relationship between the witness and Vlado Santic, and a great deal of information which is irrelevant, at least in terms of that which the Prosecutor seeks to prove. There is no contest that the witness knows Vlado Santic. It is not contested that he has known him for quite some time. It's also not contested that they both belong to the same unit of the military police, with the task, as this witness said, to guard the headquarters in the Vitez Hotel round the clock. It is also not contested that Vlado Santic, for a given period of time, was commander. However, ultimately the Prosecutor himself admits this when he analyses this witness's statement. The witness, on the 1st of April, 1993, left Vitez and the area, and he cannot say anything about the events of the 16th of April. In order to support his thesis about the reliability of this witness, the Prosecutor says in his final brief that there is no animosity between Vlado Santic and this witness. That is not true. On the contrary. There is an animosity and quite an animosity at that. Of course, this casts a shadow of doubt on the reliability of that witness. I shall remind you that the witness admitted here before you that together with a few other persons, he threw a grenade at a kiosk that was owned by Vlado Santic's wife. He said so in this courtroom. Moreover, he said that he had kissed her before that. What does that mean, Your Honours? Is there -- is there some revenge involved in that? Isn't there something that has to bring into question all of this related to Vlado Santic? However, the key argument that the Prosecutor does not contest is that this witness left the area of Vitez, and that is what is of decisive importance and everything that could be linked to the testimony of this witness. I shall not go into an in-depth analysis which would show that the Prosecutor relies on inaccurate data. I shall illustrate this by pointing out the following: When a certain person named Bralo was in prison, Vlado Santic, according to the statement of this witness, was the one who had mistreated him. However, the witness said that this was done by Pasko Ljubicic. He actually expected help from him but he did not get it. Nevertheless, I would like to say, in relation to this witness, in conclusion, that you can see that this witness stated, in terms of his own relationship with Vlado Santic, that everything that was bad in their relationship is not a consequence of the fact that he was a Muslim. Vlado treated all equally. I shall particularly like to draw your attention to the fact that this witness, and I'm talking all within the context of the Prosecutor's thesis on the persecution of witness [sic], that this witness, in response to direct questions pertaining to his service in the military police, the military police did not aim its activities against the Muslim -- the Bosnian Muslims. They did not devastate their property, their houses, or jeopardise their lives. Sulejman Kavazovic and Zaim Kablar, two witnesses, speak of Vladimir Santic after 1993, the 16th of April 1993. May I point out immediately that witness Kavazovic is a totally unreliable witness. He is a person who confused Vlado Santic, the accused, with another Vlado Santic. The witness described Vlado Santic as a person who had short dark hair. Vlado Santic, neither then nor now, had black hair. Truth to tell, the witness did say that he knew Vlado Santic and that he met him on one occasion at the hotel, when he came, when he was brought in. The Prosecutor said, in respect of that, that Vlado had some kind of duties with the intelligence service at the time. At that time Vlado was a police inspector. However, what absolutely corroborates this claim that witness Kavazovic substituted Vlado Santic for another person, and that is what we illustrated by D5 through 6 [sic]. If you remember this, although it is very difficult to recall each and every detail, witness Kavazovic said that he had a telephone conversation with Vlado Santic in those days, and he confirmed that this conversation took place from a telephone with a particular subscription number. The witness ascertained, in response to a question put by the Presiding Judge, whether it was precisely from that subscription number that he had this telephone conversation with Vlado Santic, the accused here, he answered yes. Document D5/6 shows that that telephone number -- actually, in that document there are the certificates issued by the post office and many others -- belongs to Vlado Santic but not the Vlado Santic that is accused here but this other Vlado Santic. So the witness did not tell the truth when he said that he had this conversation with Vlado Santic the accused. Zaim Kablar, a man who here in this courtroom thanked Vlado Santic and was happy to be in a position to do so, because he said that during those days Vlado Santic had saved him in those times of madness, when it was very important who would say what about him. However, in terms of the zone of responsibility, because the witness went out to dig trenches, what Vlado Santic actually had to do with this trench digging, this witness said that Vlado Santic had nothing to do with this. There were no lists, let alone anything made by Vlado Santic. They were taken away, and finally he came to the following conclusion: "Had Vlado Santic by any chance known that I was being taken away, he would have helped me." Witness Whitworth. It is difficult to say now what could be confirmed by this witness statement, except for the fact that he saw Vlado Santic at the Vitez Hotel. He said that he belonged to the local structures, that they were guarding the hotel, but he's not even sure of that. He did not say anything about the events of the 16th of April, 1993. So, Your Honours, those were all the witnesses who spoke in this courtroom and who were supposed to support the Prosecutor's thesis that Vlado Santic pursued a policy of ethnic cleansing of the Bosnian Muslims in the area of Central Bosnia, in Ahmici. As you can see, not a single one of these witnesses knows anything about the role of the accused in these events of the 16th of April, 1993 mentioned in the indictment. I should like to draw your attention to the fact that I shall speak about Witness EE later. The Defence is sure that it has not missed a single witness, and the Prosecutor, by calling these witnesses, did not prove any action committed by Vlado Santic, the accused, that could be characterised as persecution on ethnic, religious, or political grounds. According to the standards applied to date, those are the grounds that are required to be proven when one speaks of persecution on the basis of international law. May I just recall briefly the Prosecutor's amended indictment? He did not assist in the preparation of the attack on the 16th of April, 1993. Vlado Santic always lived in Vitez. He never lived in Ahmici. The Prosecutor asserts that he evacuated Bosnian Croat civilians on the previous night, organised weapons and ammunition, prepared his own home and the homes of his relatives as staging areas of attacks, and concealed from other inhabitants that there would be -- concealing from other residents that an attack was imminent. So what pertains to Vlado Santic and what does not pertain to Vlado Santic? The indictment would have to be very clearly specified. The acts would have to be fully defined, because that is the only way in which they can be proved or disproved. At this point in time, I have to recall that the Prosecutor, in his 30-page pre-trial brief, devoted only one sentence to Vlado Santic, saying that evidence will show that Vlado Santic took part in one case of murder, together with Drago Josipovic, and that's all. It's not that the Prosecutor was trying to spare Vlado Santic; he didn't have anything else to say. Now I should like Your Honours to deal with the Prosecutor's final brief. I already stated in my introductory remarks my very own position, in view of those propounded by the Prosecutor. If this were not such a serious trial, and if it were not the destinies of these people who were at stake, perhaps I would not give a single bit of my time to the arguments presented by the Prosecutor in his final brief; however, with all due respect, and given your patience, I am going to say that the Prosecutor's thesis, as presented in his final brief, cannot be corroborated. It is very interesting to see how he develops his thesis on the responsibility of Vladimir Santic in his final brief. Having understood, which he explicitly states in that brief, that there is no firm evidence in terms of the responsibility of the accused, the Prosecutor presents the following arguments: First of all, he says that the members of the 1st Company of the 4th Battalion of the military police, including the anti-terrorist platoon of the Jokers, took part in the persecution campaign in Ahmici and the surrounding area on the 16th of April, 1993, in keeping with their orders. Furthermore, on the 16th of April, 1993, Vlado Santic was commander of the 1st Company of the 4th Battalion, including this platoon. Then he claims that Vlado Santic exercised command and control over military police units; he bills his authority by claiming that he exercised discipline; he evoked statements of witnesses who saw Vlado Santic on the 24th and 26th of April, 1993, not far away from Ahmici; he also invokes 16 witness statements and documents so that he could, in his own words, prove the fact that there was a campaign of persecution, and he concludes the following: Vlado Santic ordered his subordinates to carry out persecution. The command was issued to members of the military police, or, alternatively, he says he confirmed and passed on the order to his subordinates. Further, he says that the crime was perpetrated by persons different from the accused in carrying out an order that he forwarded to his subordinates. That is what the Prosecutor claims. What, however, does indisputable evidence show? Vlado Santic was not the commander of the 1st Company of the military police on the 16th of April, 1993; not a single piece of evidence corroborates this. I will not discuss assumptions. The last legal document signed by Vlado Santic was on the 18th of March, 1993, but this document, however, does not actually identify Vlado Santic's signature. Vlado Santic is said to have been the commander of the Jokers, within the 1st Company of the 4th Battalion; however, the document of the 18th of March, 1993 leads to the conclusion that this platoon, if it was a part of this company at all, that the Jokers were put under the command of the commander of the 2nd Company of the 4th Battalion. The Prosecutor claims that the resubordination was only on that day but that is not visible from the document, and witness Dzambasovic, to whom I will refer again, when shown this document, said the following: He said this was not evidence from this document, and it is not evident from the document. Furthermore, not a single one of the 16 witnesses mentioned by the Prosecutor, who were supposed to corroborate the presence of the military police, or rather the 1st Company, in Ahmici on the 16th of April, 1993 said either that they saw Vlado Santic or that the people there were actually members of the 1st Company of the military police. They had military police uniforms and insignia, but not a single witness said that they were members of this company. Exhibit D16 shows who the leader of the military police in Ahmici was, but Santic is not mentioned there. Furthermore, the Prosecutor refers to orders. There is no order, no order was presented before this Court, issued by the commander of the 4th Battalion to his subordinates. It has not been confirmed that such an order was issued orally. There is no proof, and there cannot be proof because there was no order forwarded by the commander of the 1st Company to his subordinates. There is no proof to show that at an inferior level, there were either written or oral orders issued. There is no proof that Vlado Santic knew about any order at all. I would like to remind you that three orders were presented before this Court by Witness CE. The witness, during his testimony, confirmed that these orders were issued by him, and these are Exhibits D36, D37, and D38/2. None of these orders refer directly to Vlado Santic as the commander of the 1st Company, as the Prosecutor assumes, nor is there any proof that Vlado knew about them. These were orders issued on the 15th at 10.00, at 15.00, and at 13.30 on the 16th. The Defence maintains that Vlado Santic was not aware of these orders, just as it maintains that there is no proof of the existence of any other orders. However, let us consider the situation as it would have been had Vlado Santic known about the orders. He could only have known about the orders I have just mentioned. Bearing in mind these orders, we should consider their nature. Contrary to the Prosecutor's view that these are orders ordering an attack, a Prosecution witness, and the Defence is grateful to the Prosecution for this witness, says that these are orders issued for defence purposes. This witness carefully considered each of these orders in turn before this Court and concluded that they were orders for defence. The Defence counsel, therefore, wonders why the Prosecutor concluded that they were orders ordering an attack. Even without expert military knowledge, the titles of these orders would lead us to such a conclusion because we can see that the units to which the orders refer are to prevent attacks by Bosnian Muslims, to prevent incursions by terrorist groups, to secure the command post, and specific tasks are given to the military police. Now, what would Vlado Santic's duty have been had he known about these orders? Expert witness Dzambasovic says that command and subordination are the basic principles of military organisation and that in strict military discipline, everyone has to submit to this. There is a certain degree of independence at every level, but if an order is issued, for example, an order for defence or for attack, then there can be no deviation from this and the order must be carried out in full. Had Vlado Santic, therefore, received such an order, and the duty of the military police was to secure the command post, he would have had to respect military discipline and carry out the orders he was given, according to the chain of command. I wonder how, then, did the Prosecutor conclude, in spite of the opinion of the expert witness to which I'm referring, that Vlado Santic was on the ground? Where did he reach the conclusion that there were other orders in Ahmici, that he took his unit, as the Prosecutor expressly states there? I have to remind Your Honours of Prosecution Exhibit P390 and ask you to consider carefully to what extent the Prosecutor respected your decision when making use of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Pavkovic, I apologise for interrupting you. May I just ask you a question. With regard to what you just stated concerning the orders allegedly received by Mr. Santic, are you raising the defence of superior orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I asked you, with regard to what you said before concerning the orders allegedly received by Mr. Santic, I was wondering whether you are now raising the defence of superior orders, whereby somebody who is executing orders received from a higher authority would be excused for any -- relieved of any responsibility for any possible crimes he may have committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, no, that is not what I'm saying. I am simply analysing the orders which were presented before this Court and about which witness Dzambasovic testified. Because if Mr. Santic was obliged to carry out these orders, because no other orders have been presented, then his duty would have been to guard the command post. I am not saying that he would be exempt from any kind of responsibility in carrying out these orders; I am simply referring to the four orders, about which witness Dzambasovic said were aimed at defence. I am saying that Vlado Santic did not know about these orders, but if the Prosecutor is referring to these commands, I had to say that, according to these orders, Vlado Santic's place was at the hotel and not in Ahmici, as the Prosecutor says. I am now referring to Exhibit P390 because it is in this material that the Prosecutor uses these allegations. I do not know if we understand each other now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor himself realises, as he says in his concluding brief, that there is no direct proof of the issuing of orders, and goes on to say that if the Trial Chamber considers that the Prosecutor has not proved command or responsibility for the perpetration of the crime in Ahmici, Vlado Santic can still be held responsible for aiding and abetting the crime of persecution. I think that we should briefly consider and evaluate this thesis put forward by the Prosecution. As I have quoted, the Prosecutor admits that there is no conclusive evidence that orders were issued, but wishing to show that there is responsibility, he sees the responsibility in the defendant's omission to oppose an obviously illegal order. This is illogical. First he would admit that there is no order that can be proved and then you say that he did not oppose an illegal order. I wonder what order is being referred to then. The Prosecutor says, referring to Santic, that he was completely inactive when his inferiors were ordered to commit acts of persecution against the Muslim population. So his inactivity on the one hand and his position on the other, constitute an essential contribution to the commission of the crime. The Prosecutor goes on to say that Vlado Santic, since there is no direct evidence that an order was issued, still aided and abetted persecution ex post facto. He explains this by saying that Vlado Santic was present in the place where his unit was posted before the attack of the 16th of April, 1993, in the vicinity of the village where the crime occurred, and his failure to punish his subordinates. And according to the Prosecutor, this is a form of moral support and encouragement which contributed essentially to the crime. As I have said in my introduction, it seems to me that responsibility viewed in this way, saying that Santic is responsible because he failed to punish his subordinates, in my view would fall under Article 3 or, rather, paragraph 3 of Article 7, which cannot be upheld. Secondly, the Prosecutor claims that he helped ex post facto. However, responsibility for aiding and abetting after the commission of a crime makes sense if a promise was made before the perpetrators, led by the promise that they would be concealed or their act would be concealed or their means, were, therefore, encouraged to persist in committing the crime. However, the way the Prosecutor puts this cannot be maintained. Secondly, encouraging, instigating. Someone can be instigated or encouraged before and during the commission of an act, but the Prosecutor says that afterwards, on the 26th of April, he encouraged someone and instigated the commission of a crime by his presence. He could not have encouraged someone to do something that was already done. Since time is running out and Your Honours must already be tired, I will go very briefly through the other two topics I wish to discuss. The first of these is the topic of alibi, and the second is I have to respond to Counts 16 to 19 of the indictment. The Defence has presented evidence showing that Vlado Santic was in the Vitez Hotel on the 16th of April, 1993, from 5.00 in the morning and throughout the day until after 20.00. Therefore, it is not possible that he participated in the murders in Ahmici at that time, as the Prosecutor alleges. The presence of the defendant in another place different from the place of the alleged crime is corroborated by at least two witnesses. Defence witness Biletic, who was at the main entrance to the Vitez Hotel on that morning, says that on that morning Vlado Santic arrived in the hotel early, at about 5.00 a.m. The witness was at the entrance. They did not talk much, they just said, "Hello," and Vlado Santic came to his work. According to the witness, he often came to work as early as that. Not long after that, sometime before or after 6.00, according to this witness, powerful explosions were heard and there was panic. Everyone who was in the hotel ran into the lobby, and he heard the voice of Vlado Santic. Witness Franjic also says that at a quarter past 6.00 or until half past 6.00 on that day, he saw Vlado Santic at the entrance to the hotel. The testimonies of these two witnesses corroborate each other. Biletic heard him, Franjic saw him, talked to him. They were acquaintances from before. Franjic was the managing director of the hotel. It is not contested by the Prosecutor, it seems, that Vlado Santic was at the hotel at that time. The Prosecutor accepts Franjic's testimony and allows that Vlado Santic was in the hotel at that time, but the Prosecutor goes on to say this does not bring into question the thesis that he was in Ahmici probably before that time. Although I do believe witness Franjic, for him witness Biletic is an unreliable witness, but he does accept that both witness Biletic and Franjic were in the hotel. He objects to Biletic saying that he was highly selective in remembering, that he did not remember many people and many events and that he was too much focused on Vlado Santic. But he seems to forget in so doing that it was this same witness, Biletic, only a month prior to his appearance here at the Court, that the Chamber's investigator talked to him. The Defence was also present but did not participate or interfere with the conversation. It was precisely the Prosecutor that delineated the area of questioning of the witness and focused him on Vlado Santic and practically directed him to the topics that we're now discussing. Likewise, the Prosecutor also had occasion to talk with the other Defence witness, Franjic, and when one compares the statements of these two witnesses given to the investigator or the Prosecutor here in his presence, they coincide; namely, are the same, to the effect that Vlado Santic was in the hotel at the relevant time, and I do not see what else can be done but take those statements into due account. Biletic was tired, okay, but he does say that he remembers the book that he was reading that evening. I should like to say that the Prosecutor's interpretation of the statements of the witness Biletic is what is highly selective, because he does acknowledge to Biletic that he did see Santic after 20.00 in the evening in the Bungalow, but not because Biletic confirmed that but only because this is not contained in Exhibit 250. Biletic said that everybody from the security section of the military police, having received orders after 8.00 p.m., they had all left the hotel by that time. Perhaps a small comment is in order on the following topic: The Prosecutor does admit that between 6.15 and 6.30 -- relying on Franjic's statement -- Santic was indeed at the hotel but could have been in Ahmici before that, before the hours in question, and could have committed the crime ascribed to him. Not even under these peaceful conditions in peacetime can such -- could such actions be exactly possible. So we have Santic, at 5.30, under the circumstances as they were, and as conceived by the Prosecutor, he was in Ahmici at that particular time, then at 6.15 he was in Vitez because this is exactly where the witnesses place him. Then he was, after that, in Ahmici leading a unit. I do not find this story convincing. The logic of things is quite different. Vlado came to the hotel that morning. He was seen by Biletic. And throughout that day I do have to say that Biletic did not hold Vlado by the hand. He saw him occasionally, he heard him occasionally, but Vlado could not have left the hotel without being seen by Biletic. That is for certain. Biletic was on the main entrance -- at the main entrance and he saw all the people coming and going, and there were few of them, because it was time of war. There was shelling, there were detonations all around. So this could have happened only in this kind of story. Defence counsel Susak has already spoken about the charges with which his defendant and Vlado Santic are charged under Counts 16 to 19. The only witness, Your Honours, who confirms that Vlado Santic was in Ahmici on the 16th is Witness EE. She says that Vlado Santic was in front of her door, and then she claims together with the others he committed a crime. Let us recall just briefly her statement here in Court on the 8th of October, 1998: "When my husband opened the door and as we looked to the terrace, we could see soldiers, Vlado Santic, Zeljko Livancic, Drago Josipovic, Marinko Katava, and Karlo Cerkez. Zeljko and Vlado took my husband and took him outside behind the shed." In analysing the statement of this particular witness, I should like first of all to consider what is being claimed by this witness. First of all, I have to say in advance that the Defence firmly believes that this witness is not telling the truth. No one is contesting the fact that her husband was indeed killed on the 16th of April, 1993, but we are challenging the fact that the Witness EE was an eyewitness to the event. It is common knowledge, Your Honours, that after events which are deeply imprinted on our minds, we have them etched in our memories for our lifetimes, and we do not need any expert opinions -- the expert opinion of expert Wagenaar to convince of us that, because we are all perfectly aware that that is so. The murder of a close person, of a dear person, of a husband, of a relative, indubitably leaves a deep imprint on our minds, and if this is done by a person whom we know well, can we at all doubt what our eyes tell us. The witness is claiming that she actually saw Marinko Katava standing in front of her door. Maybe she confused Marinko Katava with some other person; she was in a state of fear and that is quite possible. However, she also says that she knows Marinko Katava very well, and she claimed to this Chamber that she was 100 per cent sure that it was Marinko Katava that had been in front of her door that morning. Well, what happened then? Where is this Marinko Katava? Briefly, Marinko Katava appeared before this Court and he said that he had been at the entrance to his building in Vitez. Marinko Katava, we've already said, was charged precisely on the basis of the statement of this particular witness, but when Witness CD appeared and stated, in another case, that Marinko Katava was in Vitez, that was when the Prosecutor withdrew the indictment. So Witness CD, in addition to Marinko Katava, as well as Witness JJ, also asserts that on that morning Marinko Katava was in Vitez. Both Witnesses CD and JJ are members of the Muslim ethnic community. It was very hard for us to reach them; the Defence had no access to them and was not at all able to establish contact with them to talk to them. Witness CD is a witness of the Court; he is the one who is confirming that Marinko Katava was in Vitez at the relevant time. This witness also claimed that on that day, on that morning, Stipo Alilovic was also standing in front of her door. These stories about Stipo Alilovic you only know too well, all of them, Your Honours, but let me remind you anyhow at this point that in regard to Stipo Alilovic, his wife stated here before the Court, and this is not contested by the Prosecutor, that he left Bosnia in 1992 and came here to the Netherlands. He was a sick man; he died in 1995. He never left Holland until his death. He could not have been in Ahmici. As the Prosecutor says, this was not challenged by the Defence. His wife said that after a lot of hardship in refugees camps, when they came here, they handed over all their documents and personal identification papers, so they were unable to move round, move at all. In fact, they were unable to travel in the Netherlands in order to satisfy their personal needs. She gave us a document, C-11, from which it is evident that they had this post office certificate which enabled them to take out the money that they were receiving as refugees. They did not have the kind of money that would enable Stipo Alilovic to travel to Ahmici and commit a crime there. They did not have any documents with which to travel. In 1993, we still had a different kind of Europe, a closed-borders Europe, much more than today. It was next to impossible to obtain passports -- I mean, travelling visas. His wife does assert that her husband, Stipo Alilovic, in fact, left Bosnia because he was opposed to the war. Why then would he return to Bosnia to take part in the war and then go back to Holland? Even if we say that this is his wife and that she has a particular reason for telling that story, we still have citizens here who have said this. We have the witness Hume and the witness Groenwald; they were neighbours of Stipo Alilovic. Let me just remind you of a detail from her statement. She says, "On the 16th of April, 1993, Stipo Alilovic could not have been in Ahmici. There's no way he could have been in Ahmici because he was in Holland. And I remember that particular date very well because it was the day when I got a job," and this is one of the witnesses. She presented some documents to us here from which it is clearly obvious that on the 16th of April, 1993 she got employment in Amsterdam as a teacher, and she said how happy she had been on that day. She says, "Stipo was my friend. And this is why I remember this, because it was the first day on the job for me." Who doesn't remember his first day at work? Witness EE also asserted that Zeljo Livancic had been in front of her door, that together with the others he took away her husband and killed him. The witnesses have testified before this Court to confirm that Zeljo Livancic was not in front of the threshold of this witness on the 16th of April, 1993 but rather was on a hill in the vicinity, Kuber Hill, a few kilometres away. (redacted), DH, Ivo Pranjkovic, and Andjelko Vidovic, these witnesses confirmed that as early as the 13th, Zeljo Livancic, Pranjkovic, Vidovic, they had all left for Kuber, where they stayed until the conflict on the 16th broke out. They claim, and this is for you to assess and evaluate, that Zeljo could not have left the position, first of all, because he had certain commanding duties, he could not have left these unit and gone to another place. In conclusion, I could say the following: When this witness, EE, claims that Katava, Stipo Alilovic, and Zeljo Livancic were in front of the door of her house, the statements of these witnesses, to which I have pointed out, say that this is simply impossible, can we then believe her? Can we believe her when she says that Vlado Santic was also among the group? The witness has given numerous statements, at least five statements, prior to her appearance here in this Tribunal. In the concluding brief, all the statements have been expounded in detail and reasoned in detail, and I should like to point your attention to the many coincidences in them and inconsistencies in them, as to the major details which are inconsistent, because I do allow that some minor details can be confused by persons under such circumstances, but the big ones, the major details, certainly would stick in one's mind, there's no doubt about that. To conclude, I wish to draw your attention to a couple of other points in order to prove that this witness is not saying the truth. The witness claims that throughout the day, on the 16th of April, 1993, after her husband had been taken away and killed, that she spent the whole day in a shed. I have to stress this. So she spent this whole day in a shed. This is confirmed by the witnesses Livancic, Pranjkovic -- no, sorry, Livancic, and I believe that to be an indisputable fact. So the whole day was spent by this witness in the shed, without ever going out, without going out to look behind the shed to see where her husband had been taken and killed. Okay, we can say she was fearing for her own life and she was with her children, with her mother, and that is why she didn't go behind the shed to see whether her husband was only wounded and perhaps needed help. We could perhaps justify that by her fear, the fact that she didn't go out to see. But she asserts, however, that she went out in front of the shed at least twice in order to put out the fire in her house and, indeed, to change her clothes. So now I'm asking myself the question, she goes out to extinguish a fire and does not go to see how her husband is. It is quite clear why she didn't go behind the shed because she didn't see -- that is my thesis -- she didn't at all see her husband being taken away or heard him being shot. She said her husband was taken and that they fired a burst, and this rifle that she claimed they had, an M-48, cannot fire bursts. To conclude, a detail, at dusk, night was falling, Drago Josipovic came, together with Witness DH and with Papic, and they called the witness to come out of the shed and place herself in the house of Papic. She didn't want to go, like she didn't want to go before when Livancic had called her. She asked them, "Who is with you?" According to the testimony, Livancic said, "Drago Josipovic is here," and then the witness came out. Now, apart from that, Livancic also said that he had the impression that she believed, that she trusted Drago Josipovic, that she felt secure when he was around and that's why she came out. So I wonder, had Drago Josipovic actually participated in this crime, as she claims, how then could she have trusted him that much to come out at the precise moment when she learned that he was among the group outside and was then taken or went to the house of Papic. To conclude, that is, just in the time I have, what remains as a question, Your Honours, what is the question, after everything we've heard, the question of motive? What is the motive for this witness? By what motive was the Witness EE guided to give her testimony in the way she did before this Chamber and thus seek to incriminate all these defendants? I wonder, was it really a wish for the truth to be established, as the Prosecutor contends, or was it perhaps that the witness was guided by basic instincts and passions of hatred and revenge? Was it not that that was the generator of her testimony? Witness AA suffered immensely. Her husband was killed, her kin were killed, her property was ruined; if we only recall what love she spoke about her house, and she often said, "my house," it is evident and it is only understandable that she should have been devastated by those events. I'm quite certain, and I'm not speculating when I say, however, that it was not the truth, the establishing of the truth, which induced her to come and give testimony in this court. Her suffering, we can of course understand her suffering, but her motive, which we can also understand but cannot justify, is vengeance, revenge. We have had many persons here who have testified. The persons in question that they saw had a clean face, she says that they had a clean face, and many lay persons refer to those persons as having painted faces, but one has to be sure, because this serves for recognition purposes. This also corresponds to what Counsel Puliselic has said here, that we cannot remember better certain events from our past as more time elapses than we can remember them immediately after the event, and this is exactly what has been happening with this witness. So, Your Honours, let us not allow hatred and revenge to prevail. It is for you that the truth should reign. I, therefore, propose that Vlado Santic be acquitted of all charges. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Mr. President, on behalf of my colleagues, I should like to ask you the following: I should like to convey my own wish, as well as theirs, with due respect to your time and everything else considered, to pass your judgement as soon as possible, please. That would be it, in a word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, we expect to be able to deliver our judgement and sentence, if any, in mid January, and of course we shall duly advise you, at least, say, a couple of weeks before, of the day when we are going to deliver our judgement. This is our hope, and we will work very hard, but, as I say, we need a minimum of two months. Now, both parties have completed their presentation of the case. Before I formally close the hearing, I would like, on behalf of the Trial Chamber, to say to both parties how much we have appreciated the highly professional and cooperative attitude of all Defence counsel, as well as the Prosecutor, throughout the trial proceedings. We are very appreciative of your behaviour and your attitude. Pursuant to Rule 87(A), I declare the hearing closed. The hearing is closed.
